title: A Brief Treatise on Illuminating the Mind and Seeing the Nature
author: By Master Yinyuan
excerpt: We sentient beings, from beginningless vast eons, have lost our original face. Taking the false as true, calling the servant the master, we vainly give rise to greed and anger, create karma and receive retribution. Like the silkworm making its cocoon, we bind and entangle ourselves, with no time of liberation. The foolish, without wisdom, rest in hardship; the wise, though they know birth and death is a great matter, desire to seek liberation.

inline.s: We sentient beings, from beginningless eons, have lost our original face. Taking the false as true, calling the servant the master, we vainly give rise to greed and anger, create karma and receive retribution. Like the spring silkworm spinning its cocoon, we bind and entangle ourselves, with no time of liberation. The foolish, without wisdom, rest in hardship and do not seek liberation; the wise, though they know birth and death is a great matter and the sea of suffering is boundless, desire liberation yet find no gate. Like the six non-Buddhist masters of old, who probed the origin of the myriad things: whether a divine self, a dark principle, or annihilation. The science and philosophy of today speak either of dualism or monism. Though each claims precisely and exhausts the mysterious, all are like the blind men feeling the elephant — none is right.

Śākyamuni Buddha, pitying sentient beings who had no way out of suffering, appeared in the world to teach them. For forty-nine years, in accord with the seasons and capacities, he spoke the great and the small, the partial and the perfect, the sudden and the gradual; with utmost sincerity he revealed two roots: the root of beginningless birth and death, and the originally pure body of bodhi and nirvāṇa. Thus he clarified the mystery of life and the universe, revealed the cause of the wheel of birth and death, so that sentient beings might know their own mind and see their own nature, escape birth and death, and still the wheel of suffering.

We originally possess the Tathagata’s wisdom and virtuous form, spiritual, bright, empty, and still, no different from the Buddha. Only through ignorance, inverted grasping, and ceaseless agitation do we create karma and receive retribution; then from shared karma the mountains, rivers, and earth are manifested, and from individual karma the twelve classes of beings (the twelve life-forms: womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, transformation-born, and so on) are drawn forth. Thus round and round, endlessly, birth and death revolve without rest. Now, to return to the original and escape birth and death, one must first break through ignorance. For if ignorance is not broken, one is lost in self and pursues objects, and when one meets a state the mind arises — then birth and death can never be ended.

Therefore all the sutras and treatises and all the Dharma gates revolve around this one center — illuminating the mind and seeing the nature — so that people may awaken and break through delusion, dispel ignorance, leave the false and return to the true. What distinguishes Buddhism from other teachings is that it strikes at the very root of birth and death and of the return to extinction. And this root lies in whether one sees the nature; hence it is truly the essence of Buddhism and the key to transcending birth and death.
[Return to extinction] To return to extinction, that is, to cultivate the Way and realize nirvāṇa.

For this reason, though the sutras and treatises are many and their expositions may differ, the aim is one; the Dharma gates are broad and their means may differ, the goal is the same. This is what is meant: expedient means have many gates, but the return to the source has no two paths.

But alas, down to the recent age of the Dharma’s end, scholars within the teaching have greatly gone astray. Not only do they dare not advocate and spread the great, profound, and essential purport of ‘illuminating the mind and seeing the nature’ — the very soul of this age’s teaching — but rather, as if speaking of tigers changes their complexion, they dare not even utter the phrase ‘illuminating the mind and seeing the nature’ in speech or see it in writings, and widely publicize it. Looking into it carefully, the reasons are nothing more than the following:

(1) Practitioners of the Chan school, lacking a qualified teacher, have no one to guide them in their practice, or to point things out at the right moment, to strike home with hammer and tongs and sever their clinging bonds; and at the critical juncture no one opens the right eye for them to see the original face themselves. Most take up a single formulaic ‘hua tou’ (word-topic) — ‘Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?’ — and painstakingly practice for decades with no news, no sign. Thus they regard seeing the nature as an extremely profound and difficult matter, high and beyond reach; they push it up to the realm of the sages, dare not aspire to it, and still less dare to advocate or spread it.

(2) Most Pure Land practitioners say its method is unlike all others — it advocates horizontal transcendence to birth in the West and needs no seeing the nature. Little do they know the Pure Land is a great teaching embracing the three capacities: toward the lower it stresses only horizontal transcendence, but in fact has long hidden the essential meaning of seeing the nature within the method. Consider its practice: when reciting the Buddha one must ‘unify the six sense faculties and sustain pure thought, thought after thought.’ Is this not simply letting everything go? Without letting go, can one gather seeing, hearing, knowing, feeling all into one Buddha-name? To recite the Buddha ceaselessly with a pure mind is to use the Buddha-thought to secretly transform deluded thought. A person cannot be without thought; if not thinking of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, then thinking of greed, anger, ignorance. By an expedient, one Buddha-name replaces deluded thought, so that unconsciously the deluded mind becomes the Buddha-mind. As it is said: ‘Throw the Buddha-name into the chaotic mind, and the chaotic mind cannot but become Buddha!’ Pray tell: what is the Buddha? If not seeing the nature, then what?

The school goes further, saying: ‘Entering samādhi is the foremost.’ Pray tell: what is samādhi? Samādhi is the same as samapatti [the threefold concentration]. When one recites the Buddha and realizes samādhi, the mind that recites and the Buddha that is recited fall away at once — this is the time when the sense faculties and sense-objects fall away and the subject and object are both extinguished. Reciting the Buddha to this point is the time when the bucket-bottom of the Chan school falls out, the time of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature. At this point, what is left of purity and Chan? Hence it is said that purity is Chan, and Chan is purity; Chan and the Pure Land are not two separate households.

For those of lower capacity, there is no need to speak much of deep Chan principle; just teach them to cast down body and mind and recite straightforwardly. When they recite to the point that feelings die and the mind is empty, they will naturally realize it. If those of highest capacity hear it once and awaken, still less need be said. Hence it is precisely those of lower and highest capacity who most easily attain accomplishment in the Pure Land school. For those of middle capacity seem clever without being truly clever, and seem dull without being truly dull. Not being truly clever, they cannot easily see through worldly conditions and let everything go; not being truly dull, they are unwilling to stand on solid ground and earnestly and sincerely recite the Buddha’s name. So they do not easily attain accomplishment.

Moreover, most contemporary Pure Land practitioners only seek to spare effort, relying solely on Amitābha’s reception to be reborn in the West. They are unwilling to work at Buddha-recitation to sweep away deluded thought and habitual defilements, but beautify it by saying: ‘We are a school of the power of others.’ When they hear ‘undivided thought,’ they shake their heads, saying: ‘Not needed! The Pure Land only requires faith and vow; Amitābha will receive us — whether one’s practice is effective is irrelevant.’ What need have they for seeing the nature! And how do they know that ‘undivided thought — the flower opens and one sees the Buddha and realizes non-birth’ is a synonym for seeing the nature!

(3) Practitioners of the Esoteric school mostly tend toward spiritual powers and the mysterious, some even flaunting themselves before the world to satisfy reputation and profit, utterly disregarding the practice of realizing the essence, awakening to the Way, and transcending birth and death. They have made the fine Esoteric school utterly demonic. The ‘becoming a Buddha in this life’ or ‘in this very body’ it advertises — that is, seeing the nature — has long been cast beyond the clouds.

Our country’s three great schools are so weakened and disordered; other schools that exist in name only need not be spoken of, as can be imagined. Thus the whole, brilliant, radiant Buddhism has been spoiled by its unadvanced descendants into such a murky and wretched state. How do newcomers know where the essence of Buddhism lies! And how can they cultivate themselves, nourish their nature, return to heavenly truth, and transcend birth and death? To speak of this, how can one not be heartbroken and gnash the teeth!

What is more, Buddhism is a great teaching that educates people to know truth, abandon vain views, turn from evil to good, and transform humanity; it is the wholesome Dharma that awakens people from the dream of delusion, making them not cling, not be selfish, and do their utmost in benefiting all living beings; and it is the wonderful Dharma that makes sentient beings dispel delusion and realize truth, put down the heavy burden, and live lightly, joyfully, and with real benefit. Hence it is a great religion of immense practical and positive significance to society and state. For the unrest of society and the upheavals of nations are all wrought by the three root-vices of greed, anger, and ignorance. Because material desires are fierce and greed soars, people stop at nothing to commit graft, speculation, smuggling, bribery, even factionalism for private gain and plotting rebellion. And Buddhism is what takes a knife to these three poison roots.

As for the course of the world and the lot of humanity, both are retributions drawn by people’s own ignorance and deluded activity and attachment to states, creating karma. In other words, all are self-inflicted, having nothing to do with ghosts and spirits. And so long as people swiftly awaken, know their own mind and see their own nature, everyone can become a Buddha. Buddhism is a broad and great teaching that advocates perfect equality, with no distinction of class. For this reason, many hold that Buddhism is a non-religion.

Further, from the Buddhist aim, the perfect and sudden teaching says there is no birth and death to escape, no nirvāṇa to realize, no Buddha and no sentient beings, and every dharma is empty. To stir a thought is to depart from one’s own school; ‘to raise the mind is to be wrong; to move a thought is to depart.’ It takes no-aim as its aim, which is the true aim, because to have an aim is to fall into a one-sided view. Hence many call it a non-religion. But they forget that though it takes no-aim as its aim, it is not without a master; there is still an ‘aim of having no aim,’ so it is also not a non-religion. Because it has no aim, one should not call it a religion; because it takes no-aim as its aim, one should not call it not a religion. Not empty and not existent, not existent and not empty — this is the essential meaning of its Middle Way, which establishes no two extremes; to grasp it, one must illuminate the mind and see the nature! Hence seeing the nature is of utmost importance for students of the Buddha.

Since illuminating the mind and seeing the nature is so important to students of the Buddha, what exactly does its content consist of? How can one attain it? What is the state when one realizes it? And what is its function after realization? These many questions are what students of the Buddha should understand and urgently investigate. For the sake of clarity and ease, and to facilitate the reader’s attainment, I will briefly set them out below, each in turn.

blocks.text: I. The Meaning of Illuminating the Mind and Seeing the Nature

inline.s: Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature’, put simply and comprehensively, means: by investigating the form and function of the human ‘mind,’ to see through to, realize, and spiritually comprehend the root of life — the wonderful substance and truth of ‘the nature’ — so as to awaken from the dream of delusion, transcend birth and death, and realize great nirvāṇa. Analyzed in detail, its meaning is extremely profound and broad, for it is the very essence of this age’s teaching; one may say that the three baskets and the twelve divisions are all its commentary. Here we can only select the essential and speak of it briefly.

Before discussing the content of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature and how to do it, let us first sketch the outline of mind and nature, so that it is easier to begin analyzing and discussing the meaning of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature.

So what is mind? It is not the lump of flesh in the chest, but the thoughts that arise when we meet a state; the scriptures call it the shadow cast by the six sense-objects upon conditions — the faded shadows of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas — abbreviated as: gathered-up and arising is mind. Originally we have no mind, but because these objects are present we receive their images from each condition, distinguish sameness and difference, establish names, give rise to love and anger, grasping and rejecting, and only then does the variety of thoughts arise. It arises by gathering together with the environment, hence it is called gathered-up-and-arising mind — what modern theory calls ‘thought is the reflection of the objective environment.’ The Faxiang school’s Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only explains this: eight great mind-kings and fifty-one mental factors. To save space I will not detail it; let the reader study it.

Since mind is thus, what is nature? Nature is the root and origin that gives rise to mind. Modern theory holds it is the energy that gives rise to mind; without it one cannot give rise to mind upon meeting a state. It is without form, so the eye cannot see it, yet it gives rise to all functions, so it truly exists. The ancients compared it to the glue in paint and the salt in water — invisible, yet truly functioning. It has many names in the scriptures: the one-real dharma-realm, thusness, the tathagatagarbha, Buddha-nature, the true mind, the great perfect sublime wisdom. Only because sentient beings are deluded and unaware, not knowing this wonderful substance, from beginningless time they have combined only with arising and ceasing, turning it into a deluded mind. Hence mind and nature are originally one thing, like water and its waves, not two matters. That the world now leaps forward depends on automation, and automation on electrical energy; without energy there is no motive power; without motive power everything is static and dead. Likewise that we can think, work, create, and invent depends on the motive power within the body, and this power is the nature’s function. So though nature cannot be seen by the eye, it truly functions in everything, just as electricity, though invisible, works in all lighting and motion. The scriptures call nature substance and mind function, nature principle and mind phenomenon. But the Chan school often uses the two interchangeably; we need only grasp their depths and distinction, and we will not be confused.

Having understood the form and definition of mind and nature, one must go further to investigate how ‘nature’ — the root of life — gives rise to mind upon meeting a state; and why state arises, so that birth and death wind on without end. One must also understand what the meaning of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature includes; and how one can illuminate it and see it, and escape birth and death. Now let us divide this into five sections and discuss it in detail.
Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature means to illuminate that the mind is false and unattainable, and, stilling the frantic mind, to see the true nature.

We who wish to transcend birth and death must first know its origin. To cut off a stream one must first know where its source lies, then stop up the source and cut off the stream, roaming beyond birth and death. So how does the multitude of beings, rising and sinking in the six realms, first arise?

Śākyamuni Buddha told us in two phrases: ‘The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only.’ This means all sentient beings originally possess the tathagatagarbha nature, a universal substance — unborn and undying, undefiled and unpurified, not coming and not going, formless and spiritual; it does not belong to delusion or enlightenment. Only because beings are unaware and do not know the wonderful substance is originally luminous do they give rise to a single thought of recognizing luminosity, turning the luminous wisdom-radiance into the false-luminance of misguided cognition. They divide what was originally one awakened-luminance into the opposition of awakening and luminance — awakening has luminance outside it, luminance has awakening outside it — thus establishing subject and object. This is what the Surangama Sutra means by ‘the nature’s awakening must be luminous; this is falsely taken as the luminous awakening.’

Because of this ignorance (the luminous awakening we call ignorance), the original perfect luminance is lost, and the formless true suchness is turned into the alaya consciousness (like a man drunk with wine). Thus spiritual bright emptiness becomes dull emptiness; within it ignorance stirs and condenses into the four great false forms (earth, water, fire, wind, inherent in the tathagatagarbha nature; the world is coagulated from these four greats). This is what the Surangama Sutra means by ‘delusion and error create empty space; relying on emptiness, the world is established.’ Because of these false forms, the present radiant wisdom is turned into false perception, which takes them as seen states. False perception, enduring, grasps a portion of the four greats as ‘self,’ entrusting itself to them as its body — ignorance envelops the eighth consciousness and submerges it into the body-root. The four greats are without consciousness, but through false perception’s grasping become conscious. The true mind is immeasurable, but is sealed by ignorance and submerges into the four greats as its mind. This is ‘form mixed with delusion; the thought-image is taken as body,’ the sentient being of the five aggregates; as the Surangama Sutra says: ‘thought settling becomes lands and states; perception and cognition are sentient beings.’

From this it can be seen that the false arising of body, mind, and world is truly the fault of the single thought of recognizing luminosity (that is, ignorance). Since sentient beings have lost their true nature and take things as self, they pursue objects and states, cling to them without abandoning, create karma and receive retribution, revolving endlessly! The sutra says: ‘When the mind arises, all dharmas arise; when dharmas arise, all minds arise.’ Seeds produce manifestations, and manifestations in turn perfum the seeds; from cause comes fruit, and fruit in turn draws cause; cause and fruit, fruit and cause, round and round, endlessly. Hence sentient beings, within what is without birth and death, vainly undergo the suffering of the wheel of birth and death, and never find rest!

Therefore the human mind is false and unreal. It is only the shadow cast by the six sense-objects upon conditions, and the six sense-objects are themselves illusorily manifested by the deluded knotting of ignorance, originally unattainable. The scriptures speak of not self-arising, not other-arising, not both-arising, not causeless arising. And the deluded mind that arises from it is even more delusion within delusion. The modern philosophers say ‘mind’ is the reflection of objective matter, but only say mind is produced by matter, without pointing out what produces matter; this is not as complete as the scriptures. The Buddha said: ‘Mind is not mind by itself; because of things, mind exists; things are not things by themselves; because of mind, things exist.’ This sets clearly the illusory arising of mind and things as each other’s cause and effect.

Since mind and things are both illusory and unattainable, once we awaken from the dream and realize that body, mind, and world are originally empty, this is illuminating the mind. In this original emptiness, one is not like wood or stone, but empty, luminous, and aware; though aware, yet still and unmoving, with no thought arising — what is this? This wondrous yet plain scene — if it is not our unborn, undying, eternally abiding true-suchness substance, then what! When this substance suddenly reveals itself, to seize it at once is to personally realize the original face, which is also called seeing the nature.

Seeing the nature is not seeing anything with the eyes, but the intimate, profound realization and spiritual comprehension of the mind-ground’s Dharma-eye. The sutra says: ‘At the time of seeing, the seeing is not seeing.’ Hence to see the nature is to see through to the true nature at the point where false knowledge and false views are broken, when the frantic mind ceases and body and mind dissolve.

The Second Patriarch Shenguang went to see the First Patriarch Bodhidharma and said: ‘My mind is not at peace; pray pacify my mind.’ The Patriarch said: ‘Bring your mind to me, and I will pacify it.’ After a while he said: ‘I have searched for the mind, and it is unattainable.’ The Patriarch, following with the current, said: ‘I have pacified your mind!’ And he awakened greatly. This is to see through, at the point where the mind is unattainable (the former thought ceased, the latter not yet arisen), this lucid, knowing nature that does not fall into annihilation. The beauty of this gong’an is that mind is a gathering of the false with no real place of coming; once pressed, it dissolves. But though thought ceases, the capacity (nature) is not extinguished; one who at that moment turns the light back and grasps it sees the nature. The indestructibility of energy, scientists all admit; and the greatest energy is the nature’s capacity. For nature is formless, great without outside, small without inside; it can crush all things, and nothing can crush it. What takes rebirth in the six realms is it; what transcends birth and death is also it.

blocks.text: (II) The Wondrous Function of Illuminating the Mind

inline.s: Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature means to understand that the wondrous functions of the mind all arise from the nature-substance; from function one sees substance, from the stream one reaches the source.

A master of old said: The substance has no form; without function it is not manifested; the nature has no appearance; without mind it is not known! To put forth function is to manifest substance; to illuminate the mind is to see the nature. Hence to see the nature one must start from illuminating the mind; apart from the mind there is no nature to see. For the nature-substance has no image and cannot be seen, while the mind is function, and function without form is not manifested. From the formed mind-function one can see the formless nature-substance. Our thoughts, work, inventions, and today’s civilization are all functions of the mind. To see the nature one must see it from these functions; apart from function there is no nature to see. Like principle and phenomena: without principle nothing is accomplished, without phenomena principle is not manifested. Principle is phenomena, phenomena is principle; they are not separate. Hence to see principle one must see it from phenomena.

King Yijian asked the Venerable Bharata: ‘What is the Buddha?’ He said: ‘Seeing the nature is the Buddha!’ The king said: ‘Do you see the nature?’ He said: ‘I see the Buddha-nature.’ ‘Where is the nature?’ ‘The nature is in function!’ ‘What function? I do not see it.’ ‘The function is bright and manifest; you yourself do not see it!’ ‘Is it within me?’ ‘If the king functions, all is right; if not, the substance is hard to see.’ ‘When in use, in how many places does it appear?’ ‘There are eight.’ ‘Tell me the eight.’ ‘In the womb it is the body; in the world a person; in the eye seeing; in the ear hearing; in the nose distinguishing smell; in the tongue speaking; in the hand grasping; in the foot running. Everywhere manifest it covers the dharma-realm; gathered, it is in a single dust-mote. The one who knows knows it is the Buddha-nature; the one who does not calls it the soul!’ The king, hearing this, awakened.

Again, take the Diamond Sutra: why did the World-Honored One, before speaking the Dharma, first insert a passage about putting on his robe, holding his bowl, entering the city, and begging for food, up to sitting upon the seat? Because he wished to awaken the opportunity of the formless prajñā of the assembly, and had to borrow the formed forms of the six perfections. For without substance, function cannot be accomplished; the forms and functions all about everywhere manifest in reverse the formless substance of prajñā. But we do not recognize it; hence the Buddha borrows formed actions to secretly display the formless wonderful substance, to cause us to realize the prajñā paramita.

Nature is indeed not without existence, but it cannot be heard, seen, known, or cognized; it can be illumined with wisdom, contemplated with insight, and spiritually comprehended. Hence it is said: ‘Thus comprehend; comprehend thus.’ The secret action of the six perfections is the Buddha’s wordless teaching. Such prajñā radiating its light, alone Subhuti understood at once, and responding to the occasion arose to ask, thereby accomplishing the wonderful Diamond Prajñā Sutra.

blocks.text: (III) The Illumined Mind Is Originally Nonexistent

inline.s: Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature means to illuminate that the mind is originally nonexistent, and to see the nature that is originally existent.

As said above, mind and nature are like function and principle-substance. Function, though it has form and can be seen, seems to exist but is truly nonexistent, because of dependent-origination and the emptiness of nature; the principle-substance, though without form, seems nonexistent but truly exists, because of the emptiness of nature and dependent-origination. The two are mutually supportive. Hence it is said: not empty and not existent, also empty and also existent, empty and existent. We must not only not cling to any phenomenal form, but must also see through the illusory phenomena to perceive the true nature-substance.

The Surangama Sutra says: ‘The nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form.’ The nature-substance is true emptiness, without form; the formless true emptiness is the nature-substance. All formed colors are false forms, without substance, like flowers in the sky and the moon in water, unattainable — mere delusion. Hence the Heart Sutra says all is without: without the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind and form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas of the worldly dharmas; without the suffering, origin, cessation, and path and the twelve links of the hearers and pratyekabuddhas; without the wisdom and gain of the bodhisattvas; and at the point where all is unattainable, one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. This reveals that we, at the point where the mind is nonexistent, thoroughly see the originally present nature-substance.

In the Chan school this is the school of extinction and non-commitment. Layman Pang asked Mazu: ‘The one who is not the companion of the myriad things — what kind of person is he?’ Mazu said: ‘Wait until you drink up the Western River in one gulp, and then I will tell you!’ When thoughts are extinguished and emptiness and existence both dissolve, the true empty wonderful substance naturally manifests. Again, the master Chuquan visited the Dharma-Master of Mount Chishan. The master asked: ‘The Lotus Sutra reveals, shows, awakens, and leads one to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; every patriarch has had his own exposition. But these are each his own, not yours. Now say it from your own breast: how to reveal, show, awaken, and lead one to enter that knowledge and vision?’ He was silent. The old master sighed: ‘Meditating thus is only wasting time — what benefit?’ He made him meditate kneeling. After three incense sticks, hearing the rector strike the wood to end the sitting, he suddenly awoke! ‘How do you reveal?’ ‘Revealing the originally present self-nature.’ ‘How do you show?’ ‘Showing the originally nonexistent (all the mind’s functions and forms are unattainable; from the unattainable function one shows the true original substance).’ ‘How do you awaken?’ ‘Awakening to the nonexistence of existence and nonexistence.’ ‘How do you enter?’ ‘Entering without obstruction (attaining great freedom; in speech, silence, movement, stillness, free and unobstructed).’

blocks.text: (IV) Illuminating That Mind Is Nature and Nature Is Mind

inline.s: Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature means to awaken to the truth that mind is nature and nature is mind.

Zen Master Zhenjue said: Though mind and nature seem to have the distinction of substance and function, principle and phenomenon, examining their reality they are neither one nor different. From the standpoint of phenomena, the wonderful function follows conditions and manifests all kinds, seeming to have form, while the wonderful substance is unmoving, transcending all opposition, and apart from all characteristics — hence not one. But function springs from substance and does not leave it; substance can put forth function and does not leave it; from their not being mutually opposed, they are not different. The sutra says: ‘All phenomenal forms are manifestations of the nature.’ Though phenomena differ, their nature is one. Hence: ‘Nothing does not flow from this dharma-realm; nothing does not return to this dharma-realm.’

A bright mirror cannot but reflect images; without images it would not be a bright mirror. Mind and nature are likewise: nature is the true-empty wonderful substance, mind the formed function. Hence where there is the nature-substance, there must be form-function; without form, substance cannot be manifested. Thus form is nature, and nature is form; apart from form there is no nature. It is not like dull emptiness, stubborn and unspiritual, falling into annihilation.

Sentient beings lose their head and take the shadow, cling to form and create karma, and so draw the defiled land with the five turbidities. The Buddhas see the nature and abandon form, and so experience the adorned Pure Land. Though the true and false, pure and defiled differ, the nature-substance that manifests form is one. We need only convert the error of taking the shadow and rejecting the mirror into taking the mirror and rejecting the shadow, and the defiled land is at once the Pure Land, without waiting until death. The sutra says: ‘As the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure; to purify the land, first purify the mind’ — rightly so.

‘True empty wonderful existence’ distinguishes from dull emptiness; it is putting forth function from the substance. Because of true emptiness, it can accord with conditions; because of wonderful existence, it can function. ‘Wonderful existence true emptiness’ distinguishes from real existence; it is gathering function back into the substance. Because it accords with conditions and functions, manifesting various illusory forms, the Amitābha Sutra speaks of the Buddha-land’s adornment; because the nature-substance is pure and undefiled, not touching a single dharma, the Diamond Sutra speaks of not a single thing being established. Not a single thing being established is precisely the adornment of the Buddha-land; the adornment of the Buddha-land is precisely not a single thing being established. Hence the Diamond is the Amitābha, and the Amitābha is the Diamond — they are not two kinds.

Mind, nature, form, and substance — they seem different but are in truth one, like water and its waves: water takes wetness as substance, waves take movement as form. The water’s nature and the wave’s form seem not one, but the wave is the water and the water is the wave; the wet nature is not different. Hence one who truly sees the nature can see the Way with the mind-ground’s Dharma-eye, and the physical eye can also see through to the true nature, because nature is form and form is nature. A master of old said: ‘In the midst of the myriad forms, alone the body is revealed!’ And again: ‘The mountains, rivers, and the great earth all reveal the body of the Dharma King!’ — meaning all the existent things of this world are manifestations of my nature-substance.

The Diamond Sutra says: ‘If one sees all forms as non-forms, one sees the Tathagata!’ If we truly investigate this principle, and in daily life see the nature right within form, not treating any state as a state, then at once we transcend all existence and roam beyond the three realms! Being born, preaching, hard rocks nodding — sentient and insentient alike perfect the wisdom of all modes. What the eye reaches and the ear hears, all are the Buddha. In the Chan school this is called directly pointing to the mind-nature. Damei asked Mazu: ‘What is the Buddha?’ Mazu said: ‘Mind is Buddha!’ And he awakened greatly. Again Lingxun asked Master Guizong: ‘What is the Buddha?’ Guizong said: ‘I now tell you, but I fear you will not believe!’ Lingxun said: ‘Your sincere word — how would I dare not believe!’ Guizong said: ‘You yourself are it!’ And he awakened. See how decisive! How direct! How joyful!

blocks.text: (V) Illuminating That the Mind-Nature Abides Nowhere

inline.s: Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature means to illuminate that the mind-nature abides nowhere, not a single thing is established, and one returns to having nothing attained.

The mind-nature is originally empty and spiritual, abiding nowhere, and only so becomes wonderful function; the moment it abides somewhere it becomes a nest and rut. It originally has not a single thing; speaking of empty or existent, delusion or awakening, true or false, are all oppositions and idle talk. If one thoroughly awakens to the source of mind and sees the true nature, since delusion does not exist, where could awakening stand? Not establishing is also not not-establishing; not a single dharma is attainable. Hence the emptiness of self is not true emptiness; one must have the emptiness of dharmas, and furthermore the emptiness of emptiness, before truly arriving home. As the ancients said: having nothing accomplished, nothing attained, nothing cultivated, nothing realized — only this is true accomplishment. If one thinks one has a dharma to attain and a Way to accomplish, one has fallen into the dharma-clinging of the sage-stage. At the least one cannot end birth and death; even ending the segmental birth and death, one can never end the transformation birth and death, because dharma-clinging is its obstacle. At the greatest one goes mad and becomes a demon, with unthinkable consequences!

The saying about no cultivation, no attainment, no realization is the transcendent speech of one who has awakened and arrived home, and also the ground-teaching of one who first understands the Tathagata’s secret cause. Because sentient beings are originally the Buddha, not made so by cultivation. Only through non-awareness, losing self and pursuing objects, chasing external states, do they sink to being sentient beings. Now if one sharply awakens, like a dark room of a thousand years lit by a single lamp, one returns to the original nature — what cultivation or realization can be spoken of? Hence one does not need toil and painstaking realization. But if one’s habitual defilements are deep and clinging grave, though one understands this principle, the mind arises when meeting a state, and then there is indeed the unsparing, fine, continuous work of sweeping! Again, if one only understands the principle but has not personally seen the self-nature, and merely has the cause for future buddhahood, one must the more diligently cultivate to realize it. Do not on any account speak big, deceive yourself and others, and deny cultivation and realization only to meet a reckless disaster.

Thoroughly awakening to the mind-nature, not a single dharma is established, no Buddha and no sentient beings; all day as if foolish, moving freely with conditions — all is Buddha-work. Smiling and laughing, anger and abuse, coughing and waving the arm — all are the ocean-seal radiating light; putting on clothes and eating, carrying water and firewood — none are not spiritual powers! In all this there is nothing grasped and nothing rejected, hence it is called returning to having nothing attained.

The moment one has something one esteems, one blocks the gate of one’s own awakening. Hence the great masters of the Chan lineage are all skilled at untying the bonds and loosening the fetters for others, having students put down their heavy burdens and open the gate of awakening. Thus when Mazu saw that some had fallen into his earlier answer, “this very mind is Buddha,” he answered a monk who asked again, “What is Buddha?” with “Not mind, not Buddha!” And Master Linji, fearing that people would settle upon “the true person of no rank on the lump of red flesh,” pushed away the monk who asked again, “What is the true person of no rank on the lump of red flesh?” saying, “The true person of no rank — what is he but a dried shit-stick?” Again, in the second gongan told in section four, when Lingxun had an insight beneath those words and pressed further, asking, “How shall I guard it?” Guizong answered, “With one film before the eye, sky-flowers tumble down in confusion!” These examples show very well that the true nature abides nowhere and establishes not a single thing. So if we would awaken thoroughly to the true mind, we must not seek by clinging to the Buddha, and still less may we cling to supernormal powers and the mysterious and wondrous!

Zhaozhou said, “The word ‘Buddha’ — I do not like to hear it!” Later people have faulted him for still falling into “there is a disliking present.” Yet Zhaozhou’s intent was to be done with the view of dharma, to show people that not a single dharma is obtainable and that there is nothing to lean upon; it is not a matter of liking or disliking. As for the fault of putting things into words: whenever there is speech, there is bound to be a trace. It is like the sacred turtle sweeping its tail to wipe out its tracks: the tracks are gone, but it has fallen into the sweeping. That is why the great masters of the Chan lineage, when they came to the final word, had no way to open their mouths, and simply shook out their sleeves and returned to the abbot’s quarters, thereby showing the final word.

To sum up all that has been said: illuminating the mind and seeing the nature is truly the guiding principle of Buddhism and the standard for students of the Buddha’s way! If we truly wish to escape birth-and-death and accomplish the great Way, then no matter which school we practice, we must strive and press forward toward this great goal of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature! We must never retreat out of fear of difficulty! For the gate-facilities and methods of practice of every school are none of them anything but means of stilling the mind and stopping thoughts, and these means all take illuminating the mind and seeing the nature as their aim. Thus illuminating the mind and seeing the nature is the general principle of all the schools of Buddhism; to practice without relying on this general principle is not to be a Buddhist at all! Again, our having birth-and-death is due to ignorance and non-awakening. If now we do not awaken, break through ignorance, and give forth the light of wisdom, how can we end birth-and-death? So illuminating the mind and seeing the nature is the crucial pass for ending birth-and-death, the pivot for realizing the great Way. Buddhists of any school must not merely refrain from ignoring it, denying it, or straying from it; they must exhaust their own wisdom, courage, and energy in strenuous effort to realize this magnificent goal!

blocks.text: 2. The Realization of Illuminating the Mind and Seeing the Nature

inline.s: Having discussed in detail the meaning of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature, we know deeply how immensely it concerns Buddhism. If Buddhists everywhere would practice it, spread it, and promote it, Buddhism would flourish and prosper. Otherwise, Buddhism would be at its last gasp and never recover. For the rise and fall, the prosperity and decline, of a religion depend upon what its spiritual substance is. If there is only outward form and no essential content, that religion is certain to decline. Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature is Buddhism’s general principle, the very place of its essence! Hence all schools and every Dharma-gate revolve around it, and in skillful and expedient accord with the differing habits and the varying capacities of sentient beings they establish a rich variety of methods of practice, so as to carry it forward and make it shine. The methods are many, the aim is one. If practitioners do not cultivate earnestly and reverently according to the rituals laid down and the Dharma-gates established by their own school, but occupy themselves only with burning incense, bowing, and seeking a few blessings, then they cannot attain the true purport of their school — illuminating the mind and seeing the nature. And unable to illuminate the mind and see the nature, they naturally cannot reach the true aim of learning Buddhism. If Buddhism’s spiritual aim cannot be made manifest, how could it fail to wither and decline day by day? Therefore, if we would revive Buddhism, we must promote illuminating the mind and seeing the nature!

What method, then, can bring us to the goal of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature? And which method is the swiftest and simplest to practice? In order to suit the preferences of practitioners of the three capacities — superior, middling, and inferior — and to help people of differing habits enter the gate quickly, I shall select the simplest, swiftest, and most convenient methods of practice from the three schools of Chan, Pure Land, and Esoteric, and describe them in detail below. As for the other schools, as was said above, they have only the name and not the reality, and have no one who truly practices them. The Tiantai school, for instance, has its Dharma-gate of calm abiding and insight, yet today its practitioners all cultivate Pure Land. The Huayan school has the three contemplations of Huayan, but its practitioners enter either Chan or Pure Land and no longer cultivate contemplation. The Faxiang school likewise has its contemplation of consciousness-only, but its practitioners today discuss doctrine, analyze names and forms, and pursue Buddhist studies without entering contemplation, to the point of dividing the river and drinking apart from the nature schools, arguing endlessly. As for the rest, such as the Three Treatises school, even their names are gradually fading from people’s memory, so I shall set them aside for now and not discuss them.

When it comes to illuminating the mind and seeing the nature, no method is simpler or swifter than Chan. For Chan is a special transmission outside the teachings, not established upon words; it points directly at the human mind, and one sees the nature and becomes a Buddha. It is not like the other schools, which go round the bend to set up many rituals and rules, having practitioners practice step by step, in order, gradually and slowly attaining realization. Suppose one would go deep into a treasury of jewels: Chan has only one door, and once it is opened one may enter; whereas the other schools have at least two doors, and some no fewer than three or four.

Hence the Chan school is the orthodox school of Buddhism: its house style is high and steep, its spirit vast and powerful; talents have come forth in every generation, the scene is endlessly various, and it alone is called the Chan gate. The flourishing of Chinese Buddhism depended entirely upon this school as the pillar in midstream, bearing the chief beam alone. But alas, in recent times this one gate of no-gate seems to have been walled up. Not only has this school dwindled in talent, utterly lacking the dragon-vital, tiger-alive bearing of the great masters of old — their means of letting go and seizing, of killing and giving life for others’ sake — it no longer possesses the wondrous hand that points out according to the moment and awakens people as conditions arise. The so-called Chan of recent times, from south to north and east to west, throughout the land, teaches people only to investigate one rigid, dead hua-tou — “Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name?” If you ask him for some other expedient beyond “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” he has no way out, and can only say that Chan must be investigated by oneself and need not be asked of others, being unable to show another eye and hand, an ingenious disclosure that would let the student awaken on the spot. So Chan practitioners toil at investigation for decades without a word of news, and what is called illuminating the mind and seeing the nature comes to be regarded as a relic of history and shelved high away. Master Taixu said with boundless feeling, “The sons and grandsons of Chan today transmit the Dharma by a Dharma scroll, not as the transmission that follows upon illuminating the mind and seeing the nature. The so-called such-and-such generation descendant of the Linji line is nothing but a blank sheet of paper — when did he ever awaken his mind?” To speak of it, how can it fail to break one’s heart!

In Chan the most important thing is the teacher. A student can awaken quickly only because a clear-eyed teacher presses, tempers, and polishes him from the side, pointing out and breaking through according to the moment. Otherwise, for beings obstructed by karma, with the mysterious pass tightly shut and the lock of consciousness hard to open, how easy is it to investigate and grasp it by one’s own power? But now that teachers are so scarce, where shall we find such a master of great brushwork, who works for others with utter sincerity and skill? So a pack of wild-fox spirits all use one rigid hua-tou, echoed from what others say — “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” — as a place to hide themselves. If you ask him, “What is Buddha?” he tells you to investigate “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” If you ask him, “Not mind, not a thing, not Buddha — what is it?” he likewise tells you to investigate for yourself, “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” In short, apart from “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” he has no instruction to give. Thus superiors do it and inferiors imitate, reducing the Chan school to an empty name and a filthy mess — is it not lamentable!

If this too is “investigate it yourself” and that too is “investigate it yourself,” what use is a master? In truth, once it is seen through, it is not worth a laugh. The so-called master has not himself opened the true eye — he too is blind with his eyes open. To ask him to work for others with skill and expedient means is to ask a blind man to make sheep’s eyes! If one or two clear-eyed people say that one need not investigate in this way, that one may use the method of direct pointing, pointing directly to what the original face is and having him see the nature on the spot, then he slanders you as wild-fox Chan. Because he himself has applied effort for decades with no news, he doubts that others can see the nature either. He may even say: what the ancestral halls have transmitted is that in Chan one investigates “Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?” — who ever heard of direct pointing? This is to be incapable oneself and to doubt others besides — how could Chan fail to decline and sink?

In fact, from ancient times Chan never required the investigation of any hua-tou; it was direct indication. As the Great Layman Fu said, “Night after night I sleep with the Buddha in my arms, / morning after morning I rise together with him. / Sitting or walking, he is ever at my side; / speaking or silent, with him I abide. / Not a hair’s breadth apart, like a body and its shade: / would you know where the Buddha has gone? / It is simply this voice, / speaking here and now.”

Master Baozhi’s Praise of the Mahayana and his Odes for the Twelve Hours are both direct pointing. The last two lines of his Odes for the Twelve Hours say, “You who have not yet understood, hear one word: / just now, just here — who is it that moves the mouth?” This is even more direct and brisk.

The verse of Master Huisi of Nanyue says, “Heaven cannot cover it, earth cannot bear it; / it neither goes nor comes, and knows no hindrance. / It is not long, not short, not blue, not yellow; / it is not in the middle, nor within, nor without. / Beyond the crowd, one with the throng, more subtle than empty space; / pointing to things to transmit the mind, people do not understand.”

The verse of the Cloth-Bag Monk says, “This mind, this mind, this very mind is Buddha; / throughout the worlds of the ten directions it is the most numinous of things. / Its free and wondrous workings, how marvelous they are — / yet nothing at all equals the mind’s reality.” Again he said, “I have a body of Buddha, / which the people of the world do not know: / it is not molded or adorned, / not carved or engraved. / Not a drop of plaster, / not a speck of color. / People cannot paint it, / thieves cannot steal it. / Its body and marks are naturally so; / it is pure, and needs no wiping.”

Sayings of this kind are too many to cite. Even patriarchal Chan is nothing but striking a spark at the very place where the seeker asks, removing his attachments, and, where the deluded mind cannot proceed, pressing him to turn the light back and shine it inward, so that he thoroughly sees the original. For Chan is the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa; it is a perfect and sudden Dharma-gate, belonging to awakening and not to cultivation. The great masters of old all grasped the purport beneath the words and took the point before the sentence was finished, seeing the nature and accomplishing the Way; not one of them awakened after long investigation of a hua-tou. When the Sixth Patriarch heard someone recite the Diamond Sutra, he awakened at once. After he had received the Fifth Patriarch’s instruction and confirmation, when he taught the Dharma to Huiming he said only, “Do not think of good, do not think of evil — at that very moment, what is the original face of Elder Ming?” Huiming was greatly awakened beneath those words. Nothing was said of investigating any hua-tou!

The mention of this gongan of Huiming once stirred up quite a dispute. Some said, “This is the Sixth Patriarch’s direct pointing. When one does not think of good and does not think of evil, and not a single thought arises, that which is perfectly clear and does not fall into annihilation is the original face; that should be taken as
that
to be understood.” Others said, “Not so; that should be taken as
what

to be understood — let him investigate it for himself, rather than being told outright.” Each side clung to its own view, and after countless battles of the pen no conclusion was reached. In my humble opinion, whether it is taken as
that
or
what
to be understood rests entirely with the person. If one can grasp the Sixth Patriarch’s hint on the spot,
what
is
that
; but if one is muddled and vague, not knowing what to make of it,
that
is
what
. Why must one insist on dividing
that
and
what

? For the words of the Chan school are a double-edged sword: one edge kills, the other gives life, and one must not fix upon one side alone. How much more so, since the great masters of old so often used the method of direct pointing!

As Chan master Linji said in addressing the assembly, “On the lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank. Would you know this true person of no rank? It is precisely he who is now speaking the Dharma and hearing the Dharma.” Again, a monk asked Huihai, “What is Buddha?” Huihai said, “Face to face in clear conversation — what is it if not Buddha?” And again, as cited above, when a monk asked Guizong, “What is Buddha?” Guizong said, “You, just as you are!” — and so on, too many to enumerate. How direct, how exhilarating such indications are! If we too used the method of direct pointing to instruct students, instead of teaching them to investigate some hua-tou, could we not also bring forth some talent? But unhappily, many people criticize direct pointing, saying: this method of direct pointing — even in the line of Shitou, in the person of the Chan master Yaoshan, its existence was denied. For instance, when Minister Yu Xiu asked Chan master Ziyu, “What is Buddha?” Ziyu called out, “Minister!” Xiu responded. Ziyu said, “Just this is it; there is nothing else.” The minister had an insight. Is that not direct pointing! But when Yaoshan heard of it he said, “Minister Yu Xiu is buried in Ziyu Mountain!” Is that not a refusal to approve of direct pointing? Later, hearing Yaoshan’s words, Minister Yu Xiu was filled with doubt and went to consult Yaoshan. Yaoshan said, “If you have a doubt, just ask.” The minister asked, “What is Buddha?” Yaoshan likewise called out, “Minister!” The minister responded. Seizing the moment, Yaoshan pressed him: “What is it?!” The minister was greatly awakened. See how much power there is in that question! Could such an effect of great awakening ever be reached by direct pointing alone!

Hearing this, I could not help laughing and saying: You gentlemen know one side but not the other. The method of direct pointing is endlessly varied; it is not cut to a single pattern. Yaoshan’s withholding of approval from Ziyu was to test whether Minister Yu Xiu’s heels truly touched the ground. One who has truly awakened, even if a Buddha appeared in the world, would be as though he neither heard nor saw it. One who has not truly awakened cannot help but turn with another’s heels. Thus after Mazu had shown Damei that “this very mind is Buddha,” he also sent an attendant to test Damei by saying, “Not mind, not Buddha.” So Yaoshan dangled a phrase like bait to see whether the minister would take the hook. Unexpectedly, Yu Xiu’s heels did not touch the ground; at the first hearing he gave rise to doubt, unlike Damei, who, thoroughly awakened and free of doubt, when the attendant came to test him, instead scolded Mazu: “That old fellow is confusing people’s minds!” — not wavering in the least. When Yu Xiu came to Yaoshan he asked as before. So as not to disappoint his question, Yaoshan varied the technique of direct pointing, hinting that this one who responds is himself the Buddha, so that he might understand. For when Yu Xiu asked, “What is Buddha?” the answer should not depart from the place of the question — that is, it should tell him what manner of thing is Buddha, and not answer with something else. Otherwise the answer would not fit the question. So after the minister responded, Yaoshan’s pressing question, “What is it?” was nothing other than telling him plainly: this which responds is Buddha! Thus this kind of question-form reply is another suggestive technique of direct pointing: it looks like a question, but read together with what precedes and follows, it amounts to an affirmation. Ziyu and Yaoshan differ in the form of their words, but their technique is one. Had Ziyu’s affirmative words not come first, a muddled person hearing only Yaoshan’s question-form reply, “What is it?” would probably have taken it as a question again!

Why, in later ages, were these techniques abandoned and replaced by the investigation of hua-tou? Because people’s minds grew more treacherous and frivolous with the passing ages, their capacities daily thinner and shallower. If direct pointing were used, the clever and quick-witted might understand, but because it came too easily, too lightly and conveniently, they would not take it seriously. They are like a spoiled son of the rich who inherits his father’s and grandfather’s estate: never having labored and sweated himself, he does not know how hard it was to come by, squanders it wildly, and ends in poverty and ruin, dying a stranger in a foreign land. Such people cannot fathom the patriarchs’ compassionate heart of utter sincerity for others; instead they take it lightly and cheaply, and cannot keep to the teaching, guard and maintain it closely, tend the Way and nourish the nature, and realize the fruit. The dull-witted, though pointed out and instructed in a hundred ways, yet because they see nothing strange, no supernormal power or mystery, think it is not it, refuse to accept it, and forever seek the Dharma outside the mind, hoping for marvelous effects.

Though the one who holds the Dharma has a compassionate heart that aches with longing for everyone to see the nature on the spot, become Buddhas, and realize the fruit, he cannot force a cow’s head down to eat grass, nor can he accept it on another’s behalf. Hence, having no choice, Chan master Dahui Zonggao of the Song changed the method to the investigation of hua-tou — though hua-tou had been investigated before, it had not yet become the prevailing fashion. He placed a hua-tou devoid of meaning and flavor upon the student’s mind, to give rise to a great doubt. It is like swallowing a chestnut burr: you cannot swallow it down and cannot spit it out; the whole body and mind are pressed into the mass of doubt; walking, one does not know one is walking; sitting, one does not know one is sitting; and all deluded thoughts and emotional imaginings, imperceptibly, are wholly transformed into doubt. When the time and conditions arrive — that is, when the effort matures and the bottom of the bucket drops out — it is like meeting your own father in the middle of a crossroads: only then do you know that everything you did before was like dreaming in broad daylight! Muddled and benighted, contending for fame and snatching for gain — what shame! After awakening to the mind, one knows that all one’s diligent investigation was a superfluous act, since the Buddha-nature is innate and does not belong to cultivation or realization. Yet without walking this stretch of wasted road, how could one open the tightly shut lock of consciousness and the mysterious pass, and see the original face? Though one walks an extra stretch of road that seems wasted, one’s legs are trained after all — unlike those who merely read sutras and recorded sayings and talk emptily of theory: they may seem similarly clear and able to understand Buddhist principle, but when things arise they have no strength and are constantly turned by circumstances. Dahui Gao berated them as “quicksilver in the medicine-water, which flies off at a touch of fire!” This was the patriarch’s poignant sincerity in working for others, adapting to the times, changing his expedient means — the bitter heart of one who had no other choice.

Though the patriarchs established the gate of hua-tou investigation, they by no means taught everyone to investigate one rigid hua-tou cut to a single pattern; they taught according to the person, and according to the differing capacities that came to them they assigned differing hua-tou. For the power of a hua-tou lies in giving rise to doubt; if the doubt does not arise, it is utterly useless. Hence the saying in the Chan lineage: “Great doubt, great awakening; small doubt, small awakening; no doubt, no awakening.” Moreover, some hua-tou can only break through the first pass or the second pass, and cannot, in one continuous line, smash through the final barricade. So it is by no means the case that one hua-tou can teach everyone. Therefore the investigation of hua-tou requires the teacher’s eye of wisdom to discern the seeker’s capacity and give him a fitting hua-tou, so that as soon as he investigates it the doubt arises and he can benefit. Otherwise it is a vain waste of time and has no effect.

Furthermore, during investigation the teacher must be constantly attentive, closely observing the student’s progress and pushing him forward from the side; above all he must seize the timely conditions related to the hua-tou the student is investigating, pressing and prompting him, so that he may have an insight on the spot, recognize his own mind, and see his own nature. For instance, when Huang Shangu studied under Huitang, Huitang had him investigate “Do you disciples think I have something hidden? I hide nothing from you!” — a hua-tou from old Master Kong’s instruction to his disciples. Shangu investigated it long without awakening. One day, as Shangu and Huitang were walking in the hills, a gust of wind brought the scent of osmanthus, and Shangu blurted out, “What a scent of osmanthus!” Huitang at once pointed it out according to the moment: “I hide nothing from you!” Shangu was greatly awakened beneath those words. From this one sees how important the teacher is in Chan — and where today shall we find a great master with such clear eyes?

Since Chan has grown lifeless and is declining day by day through its rigid adherence to old rules, the plan for today would seem to require changing the strings and altering the track, taking another shortcut, so as to break the deadlock and revive Chan.

Judging from the Chan conditions and opportunities of the present stage, in my humble opinion we should change to directly revealing the original face, and no longer hold to one rigid, dead hua-tou, so as to help students awaken quickly. The teacher need only strike a spark at the very place where the seeker asks, pressing him so that when consciousness cannot proceed he turns the light back and sees for himself; then he should enjoin him to guard and maintain it carefully and closely, dissolve his deluded habits, and bring the fruit of the Way to perfection. Of such methods of direct revelation there are many fine examples in the past. Suppose one asks: What is Buddha? The answer: Who is it that asks? He says: It is I. The teacher presses: What do you call “I”? He says: Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are I; the body is I! The teacher presses: The body is you — then who is it that knows the body is you? He says: That too is I. The teacher presses: If body and knowing are both you, are there not two of you? He says: If body and knowing are both not I, does that not fall into annihilating emptiness? Thereupon the teacher calls to him: So-and-so! He answers: Yes! Directly pointing, the teacher says: What is it? Is it annihilating emptiness? — this vivid numinous knowing, which is without body and without knowing, and yet does not fall into annihilating emptiness, what is it if not Buddha? The man then suddenly awakens with great understanding. Again, suppose he asks: Can the original face be seen? The answer: It cannot be seen! He asks: Why can it not be seen? The answer: The original face is yourself; if you yourself would again see the original face, are there not two original faces? Can the eye see itself? He says: Then is the original face nothing? The answer: Though the eye cannot see itself, the eye is not nothing! When you now do not think of good and do not think of evil, are there still deluded thoughts? He answers: Not a single thought arises! The teacher asks: When not a single thought arises, is it like wood and stone, without knowing? He says: It is vividly and constantly aware! Directly pointing, the teacher says: This vivid, constant awareness which is neither existent nor non-existent — what is it? Is it not your original face? Again, suppose he asks: What is my own self? The answer: Is not the one who asks right now your own self? He asks: Then may I take this questioner as my own self? The answer: You may not! He asks: Why not? The answer: Though the questioner is your own self, if you fix upon the self, there come to be two selves. To say the questioner is your own self, and then to fix upon the questioner as the self — are there not two selves? The man then suddenly awakened with great clarity.

To point directly in accord with the capacity, causing him to awaken on the spot — is that not swift and convenient? Compared with toiling at investigation for decades without a word of news, the difference is as heaven from earth! Someone may say: one who awakens by such direct pointing may, I fear, have no strength when things arise. The answer: if he truly accepts it himself, then even though his habitual defilement is deep, so that for a time he may well stray, yet if he can guard and maintain it closely, like the ancients herding the ox after awakening, gripping the rope and the whip all day and night and watching so that it is not allowed to stray, then within two or three years his practice will surely become one piece and reach the state of pure blue furnace-fire. The thing most to be feared is the frivolous, slippery Chan type, plausible but false, skimming the surface: his tongue may be smooth, but his mind-nature is in truth not yet clear. And if he will not set his feet on solid ground, training the mind through circumstances amid affairs and guarding it closely, but lets it wander and stray, then in the end all comes to ruin! Still, if amid the vast sea of people one could fish up one or half of one who has opened the true eye, to be eyes for gods and humans, that would be better by far than decades of bitter investigation without news, with no one to inherit the Dharma lineage, so that one has no choice but to sink to transmitting the Dharma by scroll. Besides, considering the intention of the ancient masters in having people investigate hua-tou, it was only to have them turn the light back and see for themselves at the place where thought cannot proceed. But people’s capacities today are mean and inferior: struck by this cudgel, they die beneath it and cannot come back to life. How much better to point directly, letting him accept it himself and then guard and maintain it to perfection — that is the wiser plan!

Furthermore, Chan is the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa: attached to nothing, it has no place for the mind to function. But the investigation of hua-tou is precisely a place for the mind to function. To have a place for the mind to function is to cling to marks; to have no place for the mind to function is right functioning. As when a monk asked an ancient worthy: How should one apply the mind to investigate the original face? The answer: The original face has no place for your mind to function! “Investigate” is precisely a place for the mind to function! He asked: If there is no place for the mind to function, how should one apply the mind? The answer: To have no place to apply the mind is right application; to have a place to apply the mind is to cling to marks! He asked: If there is no place to apply the mind, does that not fall into emptiness? The answer: Who is it that knows it falls into emptiness? He said: It is I. The answer: Since this is you, how can it fall into emptiness? He asked: Then may I take this one who knows it falls into emptiness as myself? The answer: You may not! He asked: Why not? The answer: Though gold dust is precious, in the eye it becomes a cataract!

The gate-facilities of the Chan school were established by the great patriarchs in accordance with sentient beings’ capacities and the timely conditions, as befitted the occasion; there is no fixed model. Since in the past the method could change from direct pointing to hua-tou investigation, why should it not now change from hua-tou investigation to question-and-answer pressing that brings one to see the nature? For nowadays hua-tou investigation, in the course of time, has bred abuses and degenerated into one rigid, dead hua-tou; no one can give rise to doubt, so that people toil at it for decades with no news at all. Moreover, conditions today are different and everyone is busy; no one can, as in the past, spend decades investigating Chan purely for Chan’s sake. Even if such a doggedly devoted person were willing to spend long years in bitter investigation, the times would not permit it. What is more, Chan belongs to awakening by wisdom: it is by an extremely powerful wisdom that the lock of consciousness and the mysterious pass are opened, not by the accumulation of concentrative skill. If we now change to the method of direct pointing, pointing out to students so that they see the nature on the spot, and then use the ox-herding method to guard and maintain it and remove habits, thus aiding perfect realization, that would better suit the times and would not go against the purport of Chan either. For Chan is just illuminating the mind and seeing the nature, and among the methods used for this, direct pointing has abounded since ancient times; it is no new invention of today — what objection can there be? To deepen my readers’ confidence, I shall cite below one more swift and light-handed example of the direct-pointing Chan method, to show that my words are not mistaken.

Chan master Zhenjue was reading the Śūraṅgama Sutra with his attendant when they came to the passage, “If I press my finger, the ocean-seal sends forth light.” The attendant asked: What does this mean? The master said: Old Śākyamuni deserves thirty blows! The attendant said: What fault has he, to deserve thirty blows? The master said: Why must he press his finger?! The attendant said: But alas, the moment the mind is stirred, the toils of dust arise first! The master gave a great shout and said: That too is the ocean-seal sending forth light! The attendant was greatly awakened and said: Ah! For years I took the stirring of the mind to be the toils of dust and deluded thought, not knowing that it was originally the ocean-seal sending forth light!

Look, everyone, how exhilarating, how clear, how swift such direct-pointing instruction is! One who hears it and awakens beneath the words cannot but rejoice for his whole life, with measureless delight! The difference between deluded thought and the emission of light — that is, the wondrous function — lies after all in whether one sticks or does not stick in daily use, in responding to conditions, in meeting things. If one sticks, the ocean-seal’s light becomes the toils of dust and deluded thought; if one does not stick, the toils of dust and deluded thought are the ocean-seal’s light. The Sixth Patriarch said, “If at the turning point you leave no feeling behind, / amid teeming activity you forever dwell in nāga concentration.” Master Hanshan explained: “What is called turning consciousness into wisdom has no other secret. Simply, at the place where thought after thought flows on in daily use, if you retain feeling and thought and become bound, then wisdom becomes consciousness; if at the turning of each thought the mind is not bound and does not knot the root of feeling, then consciousness becomes wisdom. And then in all times you dwell constantly in the great nāga concentration!” Again, Master Hanshan dreamed that he ascended to Tuṣita, where Maitreya spoke to him of Consciousness-Only: “Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. Depending on consciousness, one is defiled; depending on wisdom, one is pure. Defilement has birth-and-death; in purity there is no Buddha.” How concise and clear these words are, like pouring sweet dew into a parched throat. How fortunate we are to hear them! If we do not right now brush aside the fog, clearly see the Buddha-nature, and in daily use guard and maintain it to perfection, what is there left to doubt?

Someone may say: Chan investigation, Chan investigation — one must pass through a stretch of bitter investigation and awakening before the great function can appear before one. The Chan of direct pointing and sudden awakening to the nature is merely lip-Chan, letter-Chan, even wild-fox Chan, of no use at all. Some even hold that though other schools may cultivate to the point of seeing the nature, that is still not Chan; only the investigation of hua-tou is the orthodox, special transmission outside the teachings.

They seem to have forgotten whether the first patriarch of Chan, Mahākāśyapa, when he received the Buddha’s mind-seal, had awakened and received the Dharma after a stretch of bitter hua-tou investigation, or whether he sealed the mind with a smile when Śākyamuni Buddha held up a flower before the assembly. One should know that Chan is the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the truly knowing Buddha-nature; it is enough to understand it clearly and without doubt — it does not lie in what method is used. All methods are merely means of seeing it clearly; they are not what distinguishes the true from the false. And these means must be adapted to the differing times and to people’s superior or inferior capacities, suited to the occasion; one must not be stuck in fixed views or cling rigidly to old rules. Otherwise it will be very hard to bring forth talent and perpetuate the Buddha-seed! On the contrary, since the twenty-eight patriarchs of the West and the six patriarchs of the East did not awaken by investigating hua-tou, but by pointing directly at the human mind so that one sees the nature and becomes a Buddha, there are plenty of people who say that Chan ends with the Sixth Patriarch, and that afterwards there is only the teaching, not Chan! So what makes Chan Chan lies by no means in any traditional method.

As for “the great function appearing before one,” I wonder just what is meant? If it means that only when supernormal powers are displayed does the great function appear, that is too attached to marks, too narrow. One should know that in the Chan lineage “great capacity and great function” means a style of conducting oneself in the world with an open and upright heart, high spirits, generous fervor, and a boldness that keeps no common company; it means accepting no acceptance, not sticking when things arise, and seeing the moment before it comes — as it is said, “Though Mount Tai collapse before him, his color does not change; though a deer start up at his left, his eye does not blink.” It is not a matter of displaying supernormal powers or not. If we speak of supernormal powers, are putting on clothes and eating food, or inventing and creating, not supernormal powers? If they are not, why did Layman Pang say, “Supernormal powers and wondrous functions: hauling water and carrying firewood”! So one can see that your contempt for everyday activity as not being supernormal power is the mischief of your own inferior nature, clinging to marks and craving the strange and the mysterious! In other words, your mind has never been empty at all, you have never seen the nature, and you are still seeking with attachment to marks. Going on like this, even if you develop supernormal powers, they become the demonic path, because your sticking is not yet cut off.

Many people hold this view, so let me give one more example to show that ordinary daily use is itself supernormal power and wondrous function, and that one should not seek the strange and mysterious elsewhere, lest one trifle with the spirit and enter the demonic path. After the five great worthies, Magu and the others, had awakened to the Way, they traveled on pilgrimage to visit teachers and increase their understanding. It was hot and they were thirsty; seeing an old woman selling tea by the roadside, they called to her: Please bring us five cups of tea. Seeing five monks come, the old woman asked: Where are you worthy ones going? They said: To visit good spiritual friends. After serving the tea, the old woman said: The tea here can be drunk only by one with supernormal powers; without them, you cannot drink it! Though the five masters had awakened, their supernormal powers had not yet manifested; they looked at one another, not daring to raise their cups. Seeing this, the old woman laughed aloud: Five silly birds — watch this old woman show her supernormal power and drink tea! She raised the cups and drank them all, one by one. Watching this, the five were suddenly enlightened and said in unison: Today is the day we truly awaken to the Way! We are always within supernormal power without knowing it, and we seek it outside. Had we not met this old woman today, we would have missed a whole lifetime! Though this was the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara in transformation pointing them out, was it not also showing us the ford across our own delusion!

Master Bodhidharma said, “In delusion, form absorbs consciousness; in awakening, consciousness absorbs form. / Only gain the root, and the branches need not worry you.” In direct pointing to seeing the nature, if one truly accepts it without doubt, one will surely put down the whole body, lodge concentration within wisdom, and in daily use be utterly dead to contrivance and free of any stickiness. Even if habitual defilement is deep, so that it cannot be wholly purified at once, and in certain circumstances thoughts still stir, yet no sooner does the former thought arise than the latter thought becomes aware, and it does not linger and refuse to go, lingering and forgetting to return. Then, closely polished and ceaselessly tempered, one will surely come to “the skin falls off entirely, and only the one reality is revealed,” and need not worry that great supernormal powers will fail to unfold. As for those who half believe and half doubt, hesitating and unable to decide, that is another matter.

If it is said that other schools, even when they cultivate to the point of seeing the nature, are still not Chan, why do the sutras clearly say, “If a person simply recites Amitābha, this is called the supreme, profound, wondrous Chan”? When Pure Land practitioners recite the Buddha’s name to the point of “single-mindedness undisturbed” and “the flower opens, one sees the Buddha and awakens to non-arising,” do they not then run in the same track as Chan? Hence the ancient worthies said, “Chan is the Chan of Pure Land; Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan.” “Chan is Pure Land, Pure Land is Chan; Chan and Pure Land are not two households.” If the relation between Chan and Pure Land is like this, is it not so with the other schools as well? For all are spoken by the Buddha, all are illuminating the mind and seeing the nature, all are ending birth-and-death! Why must people insist on dividing schools and splitting sects, you berating me and I scolding you, brothers quarreling within the walls? As was said above, some hold: “Chan belongs to awakening, not to cultivation; Chan is sudden, not gradual.
