What makes Chan Chan ends with the Sixth Patriarch; afterwards there is only the teaching, not Chan.” For the teaching speaks of gradual cultivation, one step at a time, rising stage by stage, with cultivation, attainment, and realization; whereas Chan is finished in a single awakening, and in all times and all places one simply follows conditions in broad ease and roams freely with the flow of things, with no cultivation, no attainment, no realization. After the Sixth Patriarch, the Chan worthies everywhere all spoke of gradual cultivation and discussed realization, so it is only the teaching and not Chan.

These words sound very lofty, but when their reality is examined, I fear there is nothing to them. For though the Chan lineage and the teaching school do differ as sudden and gradual, awakening and cultivation, the difference lies in the point of entry, not in the speed or slowness of the realized state. One who, from studying the teachings and opening a great and perfect understanding, realizes and sees the original nature is said to be “under the teaching”; one who, from direct pointing at the human mind, sees the nature and becomes a Buddha is said to be “in the Chan lineage.” When they arrive at the destination, there is no difference between them; both are the same. Hence the ancients said: the teaching is Chan with sound; Chan is the teaching without sound. One cannot say that because Chan practitioners today have inferior capacities and their habitual defilement is not purified after awakening, so that they must resort to gradual cultivation to finish off residual habits, therefore it is the teaching and not Chan. If one insists that only when a single awakening is thorough, with no further need of guarding and maintaining, ox-herding, or sweeping away residual habits, but sitting securely at home at once without the least straying, is it Chan, then the Sixth Patriarch, who after his awakening spent more than ten years hidden among hunters, concealing his light and nurturing his obscurity, would not count as Chan either.

So one cannot arbitrarily assert: “Only finishing in a single awakening is Chan, and gradual cultivation after awakening is the teaching.” For through kalpas and many lives we have been upside-down and deludedly active, long habituated to clinging, and this has accumulated into habitual tendencies deeply planted in the field of the eighth consciousness. Though we now awaken, alas, the habitual defilement is deep and its influence is hard to erase. It is like a stinking dung bucket that has held filth for years: once it is emptied, the stench has soaked deep into the wood and can by no means be cleared away at once; only after long soaking, washing, and scrubbing can the lingering stench gradually be removed. Therefore a truly down-to-earth practitioner knows well the sweetness and bitterness of it, and dares not speak wildly, praising himself at the least bit of insight as already having no cultivation, no attainment, no realization. As for those who at a single awakening reach no cultivation, no attainment, no realization, one certainly cannot say there are none at all, but they are after all few, and not something everyone can hope for. Moreover, the sudden awakening and sudden realization of such supreme, highest-capacity people today is not unrelated to their gradual cultivation and gradual realization in the past. The ancient worthies said: today’s sudden is precisely yesterday’s gradual. So one cannot dismiss with a single stroke those who cultivate, awaken, and realize gradually, saying that they are not Chan. Moreover, such people who cultivate gradually after awakening are, in the Chan tradition from the first, the vast majority. Even the most famous great Chan master, the monk Zhaozhou, is said to have “still been wandering on pilgrimage at eighty” — how much more so others!

Once there was a scholar who, having read a few records of the Chan patriarchs' words, claimed he had already attained great and thorough awakening. He went to visit Master Guizong and told him that he had reached the state of no-cultivation, no-attainment, and no-realization. Guizong only smiled and assented. When the scholar took his leave and was seen to the gate, Guizong said to him: 'Sir, where did that large hole in the back of your brocade robe come from?' The scholar asked in alarm: 'Where? Where?' Guizong rebuked him: 'Fine no-cultivation, no-attainment, no-realization!' The scholar's face turned red and he left in shame and confusion. Is this not an exposing portrait, shown to us, of one who prides himself on no-cultivation, no-attainment, and no-realization making a spectacle of himself?

To sum up: when we are not thinking of good and not thinking of evil, when the previous thought has broken off and the next thought has not yet arisen, although empty and still and without thought, we are not like wood or stone; suddenly turning back, we should take hold of this clear, luminous numinous knowing — this is the original face. With neither confusion nor concentration, applying in accord with conditions without the least attachment — this is seeing the mind and realizing the nature. Furthermore, the nature is true emptiness and wondrous existence, not a barren emptiness; because it is true emptiness it must have marks and functions, and because it has marks and functions it is true emptiness. Thus the nature is the marks, and the marks are the nature. If in our daily affairs we can see through the marks to the nature and not be turned by the marks; if we recognize that all things and every mark and function are manifestations of the nature and wondrous functions of the mind, benefiting things in their use without being used by things — this is seeing the mind and realizing the nature. An ancient worthy said: pick up a blade of grass and it is the sixteen-foot golden body; this is the post-awakening footnote, and one must not conceive of it as something extraordinary, mysterious, or subtle. Because the extraordinary and mysterious are themselves false thoughts; not only do they obstruct one's own gate of awakening and prevent seeing the mind and realizing the nature, but they also carry the danger of falling into demonic states. Know that all supernatural powers and subtle mysteries are based on seeing the mind and realizing the nature. It is only necessary, after awakening, to diligently remove the five hindrances — wealth, sex, fame, food, and sleep — and to receive no reception at all; then naturally, when the water comes, the canal is formed, and the six supernormal powers arise together. It is like the great bird Peng, which in one wing-beat covers tens of thousands of miles, all depending on a little strength in its feet; if its feet never touch the ground, it has no way to take flight.

If it is otherwise — if, after this account, one still dares not to settle firmly, will not accept and acknowledge — then for one who still wishes to see the mind and realize the nature, nothing is better than to study the esoteric (mantra) school and from the esoteric pass over to Chan, which is comparatively easier and more secure. Because the esoteric school relies on the Buddha's power of blessing, and seems far quicker and more convenient than the Chan school's self-powered investigation. What is more, the esoteric school has special, excellent expedient means, summoning through many kinds of power; unlike investigating Chan, where apart from the teacher's pressing and pointing there is no other method. Therefore its attainment is more excellent and quicker than the Chan school, as one who rides a carriage or an airplane is naturally more effortless and swift than one who walks. But the esoteric school's gateways are profound and broad, its ritual texts numerous, so a learner cannot easily grasp its whole at once. Choosing among them that which is simple, swift, easy to practice, and close to Chan, none is better than the mind-essence esoteric dharma, because that method is the markless esoteric teaching, with no elaborate rituals, no need to construct an altar; anyone, anywhere, at any time, can practice it. And without turning corners, without practicing the preliminary stage, without passing from marked to markless, one can directly realize the essence and put it to use. Hence the world has praised it as Chan-esoteric; though the words are not apt, the meaning is most valuable. As for its method of practice, it is left to be discussed below under The Esoteric School.

The Pure Land school is profound and broad in its practice, universally reaching the three faculties and perfectly encompassing the eight teachings. For the mind is the land and the land is the mind; there is no land outside the mind and no mind outside the land. Hence the scripture says: 'If you wish to purify the land, first purify your mind; as the mind is purified, the Buddha land is purified.' The land is the mind, and the mind is the greatest power in the universe — great without outer limit, small without inner limit — and there is not a single thing that surpasses the bounds of the mind. Therefore there is no school that can transcend the Pure Land. Hence the Pure Land can be high or low, deep or shallow.

To speak of the original meaning of the Pure Land: when the practitioner's mind is pure, then all lands and all places are without exception pure and free, and the worlds of the ten directions all at once transform into Pure Lands. If the mind is not pure, even in a solemn Buddha land one is still inverted and afflicted. An ancient worthy said: 'When the mind is pure, Avici itself is the Pure Land; when the mind is defiled, the Pure Land itself is Avici.' As for the west, it represents the sun rising in the east and setting in the west — the meaning of the result's full accomplishment; hence the great Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, through the ten great king of vows, seeks rebirth in the western Pure Land to perfectly realize Buddhahood.

One who truly cultivates the Pure Land observes the mind-thoughts at all times — either with the contemplation of Buddha-recitation, or with contemplation of the Pure Land's splendor and the sacred image of Amitābha Buddha, or again contemplating one's own body as Amitābha — not allowing clinging to conditions to abide. As soon as a thought arises, one immediately awakens and turns it to emptiness, or lifts the Buddha-mind and dissolves the false thought, not allowing it to continue. Through long focus and diligent effort, when the right time and conditions arrive, suddenly the one who observes and the observed, the one who recites and the recited, fall away in an instant; the true nature of Amitābha blazes before one, and one directly sees the dharmakaya — that is, at that very moment one is reborn in the Pure Land in this present life. In the Chan school this is called seeing the mind and realizing the nature; in the Pure Land school it is called 'when the flower opens, one sees the Buddha and realizes non-birth.' Though the words differ, the meaning is one; hence Chan and the Pure Land are not separate.

One who truly wishes to be reborn in the Pure Land need not wait for rebirth after death. One must strive in this present life and be able to be reborn right then — only then is there certainty. The phrase 'at the end of life' spoken of in the Amitābha Sutra is generally explained as 'when one's breathing stops and one dies'; in fact this is all interpretation according to the text. If one follows the essential meaning of the scripture, the so-called 'at the end of life' is not the time of dying, but 'when the life-root of birth and death is finally severed.' What is the life-root of birth and death? It is our inverted, deluded thinking! Hence right after 'at the end of life,' the Amitābha Sutra says the mind is not inverted and that Buddha appears before one. When we apply effort in contemplation or Buddha-recitation and reach the point of full force, walking without knowing we walk, sitting without knowing we sit, single-minded and absorbed, with no thought at all apart from the Buddha-mind — this life-root of birth and death, the false thought, is about to be severed. At the last, suddenly the sense faculties and their objects fall away, the mind is single and unconfused, and at that very moment one directly sees the true Buddha and is reborn in the Pure Land.

At that time one realizes that Saha is itself Sukhavati and Sukhavati is itself Saha; the usual distinguishing of east and west, of pure and defiled, is all like dreaming in broad daylight. Hence it is said that one truly reborn in the Pure Land is reborn without rebirth, gone without going. If there is still a distinction between Saha and Sukhavati, between the Pure Land and the defiled land, this is precisely because the mind is not yet pure and the false thoughts are not yet exhausted.

It is a pity that at the present stage those who cultivate the Pure Land generally set their sights on the lowest level, beginning their practice from the lowest place, and all say in one accord: 'We cultivate the Pure Land school, aiming at rebirth in the West, and rebirth in the West is effected by relying on the Buddha's compassionate power of reception — it is other-powered practice, not self-powered cultivation of the Chan school, and there is no need to see the mind and realize the nature.' If one asks them: 'What is single-mindedness?' 'Why does the Amitābha Sutra speak of "upholding the name for one day up to seven days, attaining single-mindedness"?' they immediately say, 'No need, no need.' Master Ouyi of Lingfeng said: 'Whether one is reborn or not depends entirely on whether there is faith and vow.' We have only to possess true faith and earnest vows, and at death Amitābha Buddha will naturally come to receive and guide us to rebirth in the West. As long as one can be reborn in the West, even in the lowest grade of the lowest level, or even in the border-land of doubt, the vow is satisfied. For once one reaches the West, becoming a Buddha is merely a matter of faster or slower, longer or shorter; ultimately one attains the stage of one more birth and is assured of becoming a Buddha. Compared with sinking in the six realms in Saha, this is better beyond comparison by thousands and tens of thousands of times.

Because such an easy calculation can be made, some good men and faithful women often push the responsibility for rebirth in the West onto Amitābha Buddha, unwilling to practice earnestly and advance with vigor themselves. Apart from the two daily recitation periods, morning and evening, they do not at all follow the ancients' methods of practice — densely upholding the Buddha-name to sweep away false thoughts, transform habitual tendencies, purify the ground of the mind, and lay up provisions for rebirth. Little do they know that Master Ouyi's words are two paired sentences that must never be split apart and taken out of context. For faith, vow, and practice are the three essential requirements of Pure Land cultivation, and none of them can be lacking. On this principle the Pure Land masters have spoken very clearly: without faith and vow, one cannot connect with the Buddha's compassionate vow-power and be reborn in the West; without practice, not only can one not express true faith and earnest vow, but one also cannot complete faith and vow. Hence the Master, having spoken above of faith and vow, next says: 'The higher or lower grade depends entirely on the depth of holding the name.' That is to say, to be reborn in the highest grade of the highest level certainly requires very deep cultivation and merit; but even the lowest grade of the lowest level requires a corresponding measure of cultivation before one can attain rebirth. For a weak practice is precisely an untrue faith and an unearnest vow. It is not the case that anyone who murmurs the Buddha-name with an impure mind can be reborn. All the more so, the Master's statement above was directed at those of his time who sought concentration through Buddha-recitation without thinking of rebirth in the West.

Master Yongming Shou says: 'When a practitioner's pure karma has matured, the ground of the mind is pure, and one is in accord with the Buddha — only then does one see the Buddha appear before one, receiving and guiding one to rebirth in the West.' Though the Buddha appears, in reality there is no coming or going. Like the moon in the sky, in a thousand rivers and ten thousand waters it appears all at once; yet the moon itself is not divided. The mind is like the water: if the mind is not pure, it is like muddy water; though the moon is in the sky, its reflection does not appear. Therefore, for one whose mind is inverted and confused, though the Buddha emits light and comes to receive, it is like one born blind who cannot see the sun.

According to the esoteric (mantra) school, Amitābha Buddha is one who arouses the great compassion without conditions, receiving everyone and saving every being. Whatever sentient being at the time of death, he regards all equally, emitting light to shine universally and receiving them to be reborn in the West. Only because sentient beings' hindrances are heavy are they unable to be received. What is worse, because the Buddha's light is blazing bright, they fear it and flee, darting into the evil paths — is this not pitiable and lamentable!

Therefore, to truly be reborn in the West, one must work earnestly with one's feet on the ground; one must never seek ease and shirk hardship, pushing the responsibility for rebirth in the West solely onto Amitābha Buddha. Otherwise, why did the Contemplation Sutra teach us various methods of entering contemplation, and the Amitābha Sutra again teach us to uphold the name, up to single-mindedness?

Contemplation of an image or a mental image requires a fairly subtle mind, and the effort is harder than that of holding the name and reciting the Buddha. Hence in recent times Pure Land practitioners have practiced only the holding of the name. Now let us speak of the method and mystery of this practice of holding the name and reciting the Buddha. Śākyamuni Buddha, silently observing that sentient beings in the Dharma-ending age are deeply defiled, and that it is hard for them to open the mysterious gate and the lock of consciousness and attain liberation from suffering to bliss, from his compassionate mind applied his vast wisdom and cleverly established a single door of Buddha-recitation, placing one pure Buddha-jewel — the all-virtuous great name — into sentient beings' deluded, defiled minds, to secretly transfer their inverted, deluded thinking, and sever the root-stock of birth and death from the nearest point, so that the flower of the mind opens, the Buddha-nature is seen, and one is reborn in the Pure Land. All is created by the mind alone, and humans cannot be without thought; if one does not think of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one will think of greed, anger, and delusion. Thinking of greed, anger, and delusion, the evil karma of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct arises; when evil karma arises, the cycle of birth and death never ceases. The Buddha, accordingly guiding with the circumstances, seized upon sentient beings' tendency to be unable to be without thought, and with skillful, expedient means used one Buddha-thought to replace false thoughts, so that people, unwittingly, turn false thought into Buddha-thought, and exchange the defiled mind for the pure mind, thereby easily attaining rebirth in the Pure Land and escaping birth and death. An ancient worthy said: 'Cast the clear jewel into muddy water, and the muddy water cannot but become clear; cast the Buddha-name into a confused mind, and the confused mind cannot but become Buddha.' Master Lianchi (Zhuhong) said: 'Buddha-recitation is the most intimate and most simple transformation made at the very point of sentient beings' birth and death (the deluded mind).' If we do not comprehend the profound mind and the great teaching of the Buddha and the patriarchs, earnestly using the merit of Buddha-recitation to transform ourselves, but rely solely on the power of Amitābha's vow to receive us to rebirth, how can we reach the goal? An ancient worthy said: Single cultivation (relying only on Amitābha's vow-power) makes rebirth in the West hard; dual cultivation (one's own effort in accord with the Buddha's power) makes rebirth in the West easy. This is truly an immortal saying!

Once we understand the function of Buddha-recitation and the principle of rebirth in the West, we know that the method of Buddha-recitation taught by Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta, 'to gather all the six faculties and sustain the pure thought continuously,' is an absolutely certain, unchangeable, supreme saying. People of the superior, middle, and inferior faculties, no matter which, must all follow this certain instruction: within, body and mind, and without, the world — let go of everything, gather the six faculties of eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind all onto a single Buddha-name, and uphold it densely and continuously. Then naturally, unwittingly, one transforms the deluded mind into the Buddha-mind, and in the West responds to and is at one with Amitābha, becoming a single whole. Hence the ancients said: 'Ten thousand who cultivate, ten thousand go.'

In reciting the Buddha, one must neither be over-hasty, chasing after the number of recitations — lest one damage the breath and deplete the blood — nor be careless and slow, letting false thoughts find a gap; one must neither seek single-mindedness directly, lest delusion be added to delusion, nor take the 'unbroken field' of Buddha-recitation to be hard and shrink back in fear. If we truly see through the mundane world, know that all is illusion, and are without the least attachment, then surely we can grip firmly a single Buddha-name, applying effort to uphold it, and not be mouth-reciting while the mind is scattered, with false thoughts churning ceaselessly. If in reciting the Buddha we can put forth effort like pushing a heavy cart up a hill, each phrase connected to the next, each word distinct — then even a person of the lowest faculty need not fear that the Buddha-mind cannot form an unbroken field, nor that the mind will not open in awakening. For the skill of Buddha-recitation lies not in understanding deep and subtle principles, but in valuing single-mindedness. If the mind does not run outward, one can let go of everything, and with a settled, fixed mind recite the Buddha wholeheartedly; through long practice, when the skill is pure, what anxiety that the deluded mind will not dissolve, and what anxiety that the Buddha-nature will not be seen! Hence it is said: A person of the lowest faculty has the highest wisdom. For to see through the mundane world, let go of everything, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha — that is the highest wisdom.

The Pure Land masters instruct people not to worry about whether there is single-mindedness, nor to ask about seeing the mind and realizing the nature. Only recite calmly and steadily, straightforwardly, and naturally, when the water comes, the canal is formed. First, they fear that if we demand single-mindedness or seeing the mind and realizing the nature we add delusion to delusion and instead ruin our own affairs; second, they fear that if the demand is too high, timid sentient beings will be overawed and, knowing the difficulty, retreat, not daring to advance in cultivation. It is not that the door of Buddha-recitation does not require single-mindedness, or is unrelated to seeing the mind and realizing the nature. The Pure Land school embeds the profound principle within ordinary practice, and within the true action quietly accords with the wonder of the Way. Hence people of the superior, middle, and inferior faculties, following its instruction and reciting the Buddha plainly, can all see the nature. Not like the Chan school, which takes in only the superior faculties with sharp wisdom, while those of the middle and inferior faculties have no way to inquire — hence this gateway is profound and broad.

Some might say that this is the Chan school's way of speaking, and is inconsistent with the rules of the Pure Land school. For the sake of increasing the reader's faith, I quote here a passage from Master Yinguang's Buddha-Recitation Samādhi, to prove that my words are not wrong:

If we speak of the method of realizing samādhi, then when reciting the Buddha, one must at that moment turn back and contemplate, focusing on a single realm, not letting the mind run outward. Thought after thought, watch over the source of the mind; mind after mind, be in accord with the Buddha's essence. Turn back the recitation to recite; turn back the contemplation to contemplate; the recitation is the contemplation and the contemplation is the recitation. Make the whole recitation the contemplation, and the whole contemplation the recitation; there is no recitation outside the contemplation, and no contemplation outside the recitation. Though the contemplation and recitation are as mingled as water and milk, one has not yet probed to the root! One must, on this single thought of Namo Amitābha Buddha, investigate and contemplate layer upon layer, sharpening it intensely; the more one investigates, the sharper it becomes; the more one lifts it, the more intimate it is. Until, when the effort is at its utmost and the skill is pure, suddenly the recitation and thought together fall away, and one realizes and enters the realm of no-thought yet not-without-thought. That is what is meant by: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly free of the faculties and their objects; the essence is revealed as true and eternal, not confined to words; the mind-nature is undefiled, originally perfect and complete; only apart from false thought, one is the thusness Buddha." This is what is spoken of. When the practice reaches this point, the Buddha-recitation has obtained the method; response and the Way are in mutual accord, and it is just the time to apply force. Its appearance is like clouds scattering from the vast sky and the blue heavens being fully revealed. Directly seeing the original, there is originally nothing seen; the seeing of no-seeing — this is called true seeing. At this point the sound of streams and the form of mountains are all the truth of the ultimate meaning; the cawing of crows and the chatter of magpies are nothing but the supreme true vehicle. Vividly responding to all dharmas yet not dwelling in a single dharma; brightly illuminating all realms yet without a single thing. Speaking of its function, it is like the rising sun, full, bright, and clear. Speaking of its essence, it is like the setting of the bright moon, pure, clear, and still. That is illumination, that is stillness; that is stillness, that is illumination; both preserved and both forgotten, transcendent and perfectly harmonious. Like snow covering a thousand mountains, like the sea swallowing ten thousand images — only a single color, with no difference of flavor. Speaking of its benefit, in the present, without leaving Saha, one always participates in the ocean-wide assembly; at death, one ascends at once to the highest grade and in a moment realizes the Buddha vehicle. Only a member of the family knows the family's affairs; to speak of it to an outsider, to be reviled is surely certain!'

Friends, look at this passage: is it not entirely of the same track as the Chan school? In reciting the Buddha, not only must the contemplation and the recitation be one, but one must also investigate and contemplate layer upon layer on this single Buddha-thought of Amitābha, sharpening it intensely. Is this not the very skill of the Chan school's investigating the hua-tou? And when one investigates more and more sharply, lifts it more and more intimately, until the effort is at its utmost and the skill is pure, and suddenly it falls away, realizing and entering the realm of no-thought yet not-without-thought, and the post-awakening state depicted in the large passage below — is this not the very realm of the Chan school's investigation that suddenly opens to the original face, seeing the mind and realizing the nature? For ordinary people we now do not speak of investigating and sharpening; we merely say to recite with the mind and listen with the ear, contemplation and recitation as one, vigorously pursuing, and when the skill is mature, one naturally falls away suddenly and realizes and enters samādhi, which is entirely no different from the Chan school's seeing the mind and realizing the nature. But one must not, as people ordinarily do, regard the mere performance of the morning and evening recitation as the whole business.

Having spoken to this point, it is truly hard to find words! Even the highly esteemed Master Yinguang, at the end, could only sigh and say: 'To speak of it to an outsider, to be reviled is surely certain!' How much the more for others! At the assembly of the Lotus Sutra, when the Buddha preached, five thousand people still left their seats; how much less in the Dharma-ending age, where to have everyone believe and enter, without giving rise to doubt and slander — how could that ever be accomplished?!

The esoteric (mantra) school is the most convenient, most complete, and most timely gateway by which the Buddhas save sentient beings in the Dharma-ending age, and it is the gateway that no school can deviate from. From essence to function, from small to great, from shallow to deep, from the end back to the root — it possesses everything, and nothing is lacking. It is a pity that in modern times students of Buddhism, not attending to proper practice and the realization of the essence and attainment of the Way, only learn some superficialities and the methods of activating function, dabbling in the mysterious and displaying supernatural powers, making themselves thoroughly uncanny and despised by the honest and upright. Even the Master Hongyi, because he did not understand the true character of the esoteric school and was misled by its outer form, reviled the esoteric school. Later, after deeply studying the doctrines of the esoteric school, he came to know that it is profound, vast, and hard to conceive, and that its gateway is complete and lacks nothing; and he deeply repented, warning later students not to doubt and slander the esoteric school because of misconstruing its ritual forms, but first to deeply investigate the esoteric teachings, and after mastering the doctrine, then to investigate the practice of its rituals.

It is precisely because students of the esoteric school do not attend to proper practice that those cultivating Chan or the Pure Land all keep their distance from the esoteric school, fearing to catch some uncanniness; but this is actually superfluous and unnecessary. Because the esoteric vehicle is the Buddha's heart-seal, and even the Buddhas of the three times cannot leave it to attain Buddhahood — how much the more for later students of the Chan and Pure Land schools! If you try to leave it and escape it, it is like fleeing one's shadow at noon — merely adding to one's own toil! For instance, the Pure Land school, though it does not advocate seeing the mind and realizing the nature, still, in order to eliminate karmic hindrances and ensure rebirth in the West, must uphold the Surangama Mantra, the Great Compassion Mantra, the Rebirth Mantra, and the ten lesser mantras. Tell me, are these many mantras not esoteric dharmas? When a Chan cultivator investigates until the seeds are churning, unable to advance and unable to retreat, oppressed and vexed to death, and at the point of no help, then without relying on the power of the esoteric mantra and the Buddhas' and bodhisattvas' blessing, one cannot pass this barrier and break the mass of doubt and personally realize the original. Master Hanshan says: 'The great masters of the Chan school in every age have all secretly upheld the sacred mantras, covertly borrowing the Buddha's power, yet kept it hidden and not revealed. Now I publicly point this out for all of you: when investigating Chan until the seeds of beginningsless ignorance are churning and one is vexed to death, one must quickly rely on the Surangama Mantra to borrow the Buddha's compassionate power; only then can one cross the barrier.' Such Chan, which boasts of self-powered cultivation and realization, which proudly proclaims its lofty manner and its separate transmission outside the teachings, pointing directly to the nature to see it — even this does not leave the esoteric vehicle; how much the more so for other gateways!

According to Japan's Outline of the Esoteric Teachings: The emperor once summoned the great masters of the various schools to the palace to hold a Dharma assembly, to discuss which school was best and which attained the Way fastest, so as to select one to follow in practice. After the patriarchs of the various schools had each presented the merits of their own school and boasted that theirs was the best, the fastest, and the most complete, the great master Kobo (Kukai) of the esoteric school said to the emperor: All the schools are good and each has its merits, but none can be separated from the esoteric; apart from the esoteric there are no schools. Because the esoteric is the Buddha's heart-seal; apart from the Buddha's mind, how could there be any schools? Hence the esoteric truly gathers the strengths of all the schools and is the most complete, most convenient, and most rapid gateway, the necessary route by which the Buddhas of the three times attain the Way. The emperor deeply approved, and hence the esoteric school in Japan alone flourished.

The esoteric school relies on the Mahavairocana (Great Sun) Sutra and the Vajrasekhara (Diamond Pinnacle) Sutra. It establishes ten kinds of mind, gathers all the teachings, and constructs the mandala; with body, speech, and mind, the three mysteries, in mutual accord, the ordinary becomes the sage. Its inconceivable power and function only the Buddha can know — it cannot be measured by bodhisattvas still on the causal stages. Profound, esoteric, and secret, it is also a teaching that is not permitted to be shown to one who has not been consecrated (given abhiseka); hence it is called the esoteric (mantra) school. Its schools and gateways are numerous and are beyond the scope of this present discussion, so I will not dwell on them; here I will only, in regard to what is connected with seeing the mind and realizing the nature, select the important points and speak of them briefly.

Speaking of the esoteric school, it seems to be all about supernatural transformations. Because of this, Emperor Wuzong of the Tang dynasty, greatly fearing that esoteric practitioners through supernatural powers would destroy his empire and topple his throne, ordered the suppression of the esoteric school. Later, Emperor Zhu Yuanzhang of the Ming dynasty was even more wary of the esoteric school and strictly forbade it, so the esoteric school disappeared from China. Later people went to Japan and the Tibetan regions to study it, calling it the Eastern Esoteric and the Tibetan Esoteric — is this not lamentable! Down to the present day, students of Buddhism value not the Way but only supernatural powers, mistakenly thinking that seeing the mind and realizing the nature is to manifest great supernatural powers, and that if one has not manifested supernatural powers, one has not seen the mind and realized the nature. Such a wrong view not only misleads oneself but also misleads others. Little do they know that the principle realized by seeing the mind and realizing the nature, though no different from that of all Buddhas, is nevertheless such that through many eons and lives the habitual defilements are deep and cannot be suddenly dispelled. At that time one is only a Buddha on the causal stage, like a newborn infant, which though it is a human being, cannot yet function; one must, in accord with the awakening, cultivate, diligently removing habitual tendencies and nurturing the holy embryo; only then do the supernatural powers begin to flower. The Surangama Sutra says: 'Principle belongs to sudden awakening, and along with the awakening it is entirely dispelled; matters are gradually eliminated, being exhausted in stages.' The Mahavairocana Sutra says: 'A bodhisattva dwelling here, diligently removing the five hindrances, will not be long before the five supernormal powers arise together.' It is a pity that so many Buddhists do not understand this principle, but are bent only on supernatural powers, pandering to what the crowd likes, to display their own abilities. So students of the esoteric school follow suit in droves, taking up only the superficial, functioning methods of supernatural transformation, while setting aside the great Dharma of realizing the essence and ending birth and death — how deplorable!

Within the esoteric dharmas, each school has its own supreme, excellent method, whose power and function are inconceivable; practicing in accordance with the method, one obtains real benefit and realizes the noble fruit. But among them the most perfect, the most complete, and the most excellent is the Great Perfection (Dzogchen) of the Red School (Nyingma). This method is the highest gateway of the nine-vehicle progression, with nothing above it. Its preliminary course, the Mahamudra of the Ganges, equals the Chan school's direct pointing to the mind-method, and is even more complete than Chan. The first half of the Great Perfection, the Trekcho practice, sealing the three emptinesses, is the Chan school's seeing the nature; its second half, the Togal, in which the body dissolves into a rainbow of light, is the Chan school's upward leap. But the Chan school relies solely on self-powered cultivation and realization, with no convenient means of reception, and so the results are very slow; whereas the esoteric school, in addition to self-power, also obtains the Buddha's power of blessing, and has all kinds of special expedient means of reception. The excellence of its reception is like the principle of modern laser — very scientific — hence the results are swift and the strength is quickly gained.

The great esoteric dharmas have already been incorporated, at least in part, into the Chan and Pure Land methods. If a practitioner can, on top of Chan and Pure Land, additionally cultivate the esoteric dharma to make up for the deficiencies of Chan and Pure Land, then progress will be faster and the results greater. Master Hanshan says: 'Those whose Buddha-recitation lacks strength may hold the mantra (recite the mantra), and borrowing the power of the Buddha's heart-seal, can achieve twice the result with half the effort.' Especially for Chan students who investigate a rigid hua-tou and, without an enlightened master to temper and press them, get no news at all and waste their energy — it would be better to switch to cultivating an esoteric dharma and, relying on the Buddha's compassionate power, more easily awaken and accomplish. But if a practitioner dislikes the complexity of the rituals, the elaborateness of the contemplations, and the slowness of the preliminary practices, then nothing is better than cultivating the mind-essence esoteric dharma. For although the Great Perfection is complete and lacking nothing, before practicing it one must first cultivate the preliminaries, and when practicing Trekcho one must also perform all kinds of marked contemplations — elaborate and complex — not as simple and easy as the mind-essence esoteric dharma. Because the mind-essence esoteric dharma is the markless esoteric, direct and satisfying, with no need to pass from marked to markless; neither requiring preliminary practice nor requiring contemplations, it directly realizes the markless source of the mind; it is truly the most simple, the most easy, the fastest, and the most wonderful method in the esoteric school. But for one whose nature is inclined toward contemplation and who likes to start from the marked — the deity, the seed syllable, the three channels, five wheels, and so on — then cultivating the Great Perfection is more suitable.

The mind-essence dharma is a method of the Tibetan Esoteric Red School (Nyingma), and the Eastern Esoteric also has a transmission of it. In the past, Master Norbu (Nona) transmitted it in Shanghai to Yuan Xilian. It is a pity that, being one of the supreme, markless esoteric dharmas within the esoteric section, in Tibet one had to practice the marked esoteric for twenty or thirty years before one could be taught it; hence it was not widely transmitted, and the great Dharma nearly sank into oblivion. Now this Dharma has been able to spread widely, entirely owing to the great master Dayu (Azhali), who practiced the pratyutpanna (Buddha-present) samādhi on Mount Lu, undergoing much hardship, deeply entering meditation, and being moved by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva to appear and consecrate and transmit it to him, telling him that in the esoteric section of Japan's Taisho Revised Tripitaka there is the Buddha-Heart Sutra, Which Also Penetrates the Great Mahapratisara Dharani, which is the text of this Dharma, and could be consulted in detail. Master Yu, having obtained the Dharma and cultivated it successfully, deeply felt the decline of Buddhism and the difficulty of repaying the Buddha's grace, and, not declining hardship, came down the mountain to spread it widely. Later Master Wang Xianglu received the dharma and transmitted it; his Dharma-receiving disciples spread across nearly the whole country, and the Dharma began to flourish in the world. This method is simple and quick; scholars all call it Chan-esoteric — the words seem inapt, but the meaning truly corresponds. Is this not also the arrival of the right time and conditions, for the Dharma to arise in the world for the benefit of the vast numbers of sentient beings!

The mind-essence esoteric dharma uses six mudras and a single mantra, with the three mysteries' blessing; whether or not one sets up an altar, it is acceptable. In practice, one forms the mudra with the hands, holds the mantra with the mouth, and performs no visual contemplation, but only turns back to listen to the soundless sound of the mind holding the mantra — like the contemplation of Buddha-recitation. When holding the mantra one does the vajra-recitation, merely moving the lips and not emitting sound, continuous and unbroken; because one thereby obtains the Buddha's power of blessing, entering samādhi is extremely swift. Practicing thus neither injures the breath nor the blood, and is a wonderful method for nourishing the body. Since emitting sound injures the breath, and silent recitation injures the blood, now doing the vajra-recitation — reciting with the mind, listening with the ear, the intention not running outward, a single thread unbroken — the mind is clear and the will concentrated, the breath and blood harmonized, and one peacefully enters samādhi; the spirit is bright and vigorous, the body healthy and at ease, and the basis of seeing the mind and realizing the nature is established right here!

This method can be practiced for one sitting a day, or two; there are also the methods of a seven-day intensive and nine sittings. Each sitting is two hours, with the hands forming the mudra without loosening and the mouth holding the mantra without stopping; one must not release the mudra and descend from the seat midway — otherwise it does not count, and one must start over from the beginning. If one's faculties are suitable and one can practice continuously without interruption, having completed a thousand sittings, one is certain to see the mind and realize the nature. Having seen the nature, one then functions from the essence, polishing the habitual tendencies, and is in the same track as the Chan school. If one further uses the Great Perfection's Togal method in diligent cultivation, so that the body dissolves into a rainbow of light and one realizes the Buddha fruit — that too is not difficult!

The above methods — the mind-essence and the Great Perfection — being esoteric dharmas, cannot be publicly displayed or taught without consecration (abhiseka); hence I will not speak in detail of their practice. Those of resolve should seek a master to consecrate and transmit them to them, and practice in accordance with them — then there will naturally be benefit.

All sentient beings are originally Buddha, and originally need no method of cultivation to realize the Buddha fruit; only because their accumulated defilements are deep, and though they meet a clear-eyed person who directly points out the mind-nature, they are unwilling to trust themselves and accept it — hence they must necessarily borrow a method to cultivate, as a means of stopping the crying of the child with a yellow leaf. And among the various methods, because the skillful, expedient means differ, there are differences of quick and slow, of haste and delay in practice. Chan investigation often takes several decades before one gets a bit of news, or even a whole lifetime of bewilderment without awakening. Those who cultivate other schools also mostly dare not speak of seeing the mind and realizing the nature — the Pure Land school especially. The above-mentioned mind-essence esoteric dharma may well be said to be considerably more convenient and quick, yet it still requires a thousand sittings, about three years, before one can personally see the original face (this speaks of the slowest; those of sharp faculties who attain quickly need not sit the full thousand). To speak plainly, this is all to be innocent yet wear cangue and chains, to have no business and yet go a roundabout road. When finally one opens the bottom of the tub and sees the original, one knows that it was originally complete all along, and that this was all a superfluous act.

Between one who sees the nature by a single thought of turning back the light, and one who sees the nature by cultivating the mind-essence dharma for a thousand sittings, and even one who sees the nature after several decades of Chan investigation — the quickness and slowness of their time cannot be reckoned in the same terms. But those who have gone the extra roundabout miles are not without compensation, and it is worthwhile. Because after walking many roundabout miles, the strength of the feet is at least trained. Those who have not walked roundabout miles have weak feet; as soon as they set out — that is, when they face circumstances or meet conditions — they at once feel their strength is insufficient! Why? Because though the principle realized by the above three kinds of people is no different, in power and function there is a great difference. In one case, the awakening came very easily, without the tempering of cultivating concentration, and the mind constantly moves with circumstances, unable to be self-mastered, so the strength is insufficient; in the other case, one has long sat in meditation, with deep skill in concentration, investigating, tempering, lifting, and contemplating, and once awakened is therefore free and at ease, not turned by the dust of circumstances. As an ancient worthy said: 'Merit is never cast in vain; the Dharma is never wasted!' Xuedou said: 'For decades I have suffered hardship; for your sake I dived several times into the lair of the grey dragon. How sad! How sad! Yet it is worth telling — let the clear-eyed monk not slight this!' This praises precisely this.

Cultivating the mind-essence dharma for about three years, relying on the Buddha's power of blessing, one can awaken; though it takes more time than one who turns back the light in a single thought, it saves ten times the toil compared with one who diligently investigates Chan for thirty years, and one can obtain the same power, function, and results. We descendants of the Dharma-ending age — apart from deeply rejoicing at how, through what merit, we have encountered this great Dharma, and profoundly thanking the Buddhas and bodhisattvas for their compassionate grace — what more is there to say!

Furthermore, the mind-essence dharma, besides enabling one to see the mind, realize the nature, and accomplish in this life, can also support one who has made vows to seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. If one's Buddha-recitation lacks strength and the sacred state cannot appear, one may use this method in practice to realize samādhi, and then there is full certainty of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Though this method is named an esoteric dharma, it is in reality a perfect, wondrous great Dharma that melts Chan and the Pure Land into a single crucible! Those of resolve should seek it out and cultivate it!

Lastly, I earnestly advise fellow practitioners of the esoteric: be careful not to use the esoteric Dharma for criminal deeds and so incur severe karmic retribution. The esoteric Dharma indeed has all kinds of mysterious supernatural powers and wondrous functions, but know that any supernatural power obtained by practicing a wondrous method is not true power; it cannot be spoken of in the same breath as the power realized by the vanishing of defilements and the manifestation of the luminous light of wisdom. This kind of power obtained by practicing a method is merely dependent power, similar to the techniques of outside paths; it can only please and show off before the ignorant and petty, and cannot ascend the halls of refinement. Even if one can for a while pose as sacred and obtain a little fame and benefit, when one's eyes fall to the ground, not only will the supernatural powers vanish with nothing to rely on, but one will also undergo fierce evil retribution in accord with one's karma.

Before seeing the mind and realizing the nature, whatever method you cultivate and however hard you practice, you cannot escape the category of 'blind practice and wild training'! Because not having awakened to the true mind, one cannot be without doubt about the practice. Though one still applies effort diligently, yet with doubt and hesitation remaining lodged in the breast, the state of unease cannot be avoided. And this state of unease is the very root of birth and death; hence however deep the counteracting practice, it is not true cultivation. Master Puzhao's Cultivation of Mind Essentials says: 'Cultivation before awakening — though one diligently applies effort and never forgets to cultivate thought after thought, yet one gives rise to doubt at every point, unable to be without obstruction, as if there were a thing lodged in the breast, so that the state of unease is always present before one. As days and months pass and the counteracting practice matures, the body and mind's passing dust becomes like a fleeting ease. Yet though there be this fleeting ease, the root of doubt is not cut off; like a stone pressing down grass [which will grow back], one is still not free within the realm of birth and death.' Hence it is said: 'Cultivation before awakening is not true cultivation.'

But no one can avoid this period of blind practice and wild training. After one opens the bottom of the tub and clearly knows the original, one returns home along the road, and with conditions, settles the habitual tendencies; freely cultivating both concentration and wisdom together, naturally without contriving, in stillness and in motion always in Chan — this is the true cultivation of no-cultivation. The Cultivation of Mind Essentials says: 'Even for one of inferior faculties, after seeing the nature, though afflictions are dense and habitual defilements deep, and in facing objects one gives rise to emotion thought after thought, and in meeting conditions one's mind is ever manufacturing existence, or even is benighted by conditions and objects, confused and deluded, and obscures the original — though one still uses various expedient means of counteracting to remove the inferior habits and cleanse the defilements, which is not without meritful cultivation, yet because thought after thought is free of doubt, not falling into obstruction, as days and months pass and the effort reaches its utmost and the skill is pure, one naturally accords with the true and wondrous nature, freely serene and knowing, no different from the superior faculties of the previous case.' Hence students of Buddhism must first take seeing the mind and realizing the nature as their goal; only after seeing the mind and cutting off the habitual tendencies is it true cultivation. This is also why I cry out loudly that one need not investigate a rigid, dead hua-tou, but only let the master directly point out the mind-nature, causing the student to awaken at once, and then undertake true cultivation — so as not to waste time in vain.

Someone says: To see the mind and realize the nature is to be a sage; not only need one not further practice, but one also must manifest all kinds of supernatural powers and transformations, greatly different from ordinary people — what is called the great mechanism and the great function, with mysterious, unfathomable transformations. Why then do you now say the opposite, that only after awakening is there true cultivation?

Reply: Students of the Way today have two kinds of faults. The first is to think that having awakened one is a sage and should manifest all kinds of supernatural transformations; if one cannot transform, then one has not awakened, but is merely an 'oral Chan' — empty talk of the true principle. Hence many give rise to a sense of inferiority and discouragement, and instead fall into the fault of having no share. The second is to say that the patriarchal school originally has no cultivation, no attainment, and no realization, and that a single awakening is enough — why should one further practice and refine? As a result, though one has awakened to the principle, the habitual tendencies remain as before; as days and months pass, one goes on wandering in birth and death as before, unable to escape the wheel of the six realms. On this point I have already spoken earlier, and it might seem unnecessary to speak again; but because it bears enormously on the success or failure of the cultivator, and is exactly the root of the disease where today's students of the Way misunderstand, I do not begrudge the words and will discuss it again in detail.

The Xiu Xin Jue (Essentials of Mind-Cultivation) says: “There are many gates to enter the Way, but to state it briefly, they do not go beyond two: sudden awakening and gradual practice.” It also says: “These two gates, sudden and gradual, are the rule of a thousand sages. All the saints above have in every case first awakened and then practiced, and by practicing attained realization. The so-called spiritual powers and transformations are unfolded through gradual nurturing, relying on awakening and practice; they are not revealed at the very moment of awakening.”

Master Guifeng says: “Recognizing that the frozen pond is entirely water, one depends on the warmth of the sun to thaw it; realizing that the common man is already the Buddha, one relies on the power of the Dharma to nurture and refine. When the ice melts, the water flows and moistens, and only then does its power to irrigate and cleanse become manifest; when delusion is exhausted, the mind becomes empty and transparent, and only then does its radiance shine forth. The spiritual powers and transformations in worldly affairs are not the work of a single day, but are gradually nurtured and manifested.”

Yangshan, instructing the assembly, said: “I now tell you plainly: do not go grasping and clinging, but simply cultivate truthfully within your own nature-sea, and do not seek the three insights and six superknowledges. Why? These are matters of the very margin of sainthood. For now, simply recognize the mind and realize the nature; once you obtain the root, do not worry about the branches. In days to come, it will be spontaneously complete and full. If you have not obtained the root, and merely learn such things with the emotions, you will never attain them; and what you do attain will not be true, and will in the end lead you into the demonic realm.”

From the above citations we can see that sudden awakening means this: when the common man is deluded, he mistakenly grasps the four elements as his body and false thinking as his mind, not knowing that his own nature is the true Dharma-body and that his own spiritual knowing is the true Buddha; forever seeking the Buddha outside the mind, running east and west, until suddenly a good-knowledge points him to the entrance, and in a single turn of the light he sees his own nature and recognizes his own mind. And this mind-nature is originally without affliction, originally without arising and ceasing, perfect and complete of itself, fully endowed of itself, in no way different from the Buddhas; and from the common man to the Buddha-stage there is no further gradation or sequence. Hence it is called sudden awakening.

Although it is called sudden awakening, yet this belongs to the side of principle; in the realm of actual practice, habitual defilements accumulated over many lives and kalpas — born and dying, clinging firmly — can by no means be suddenly eradicated. Therefore one must, relying on awakening, practice to gradually remove habitual tendencies until delusion is exhausted, and only then do spiritual powers manifest. It is absolutely not the case that spiritual powers appear at the moment of the sudden awakening to principle. Hence the cultivator must clearly understand the process, distinguish what comes first and what comes after, and must not, because of the absence of spiritual powers, doubt himself or, still more, doubt others — supposing that none of them can awaken — and so take another path and fall into a wrong way. Even if he passed through kalpas of dust he could not accomplish the Way.

Moreover, whether one has revealed spiritual powers does not suffice to show whether or not one has awakened. First, there are many kinds of supernormal powers: some are gained through esoteric practices, some through the agency of spirits and ghosts, some as a karmic reward of prior nurture, and so forth — one cannot claim that all such persons have awakened. For these powers, having some support, are not true powers, or are only semblances of power; once the physical body decays and loses its support, they vanish completely. Second, the ancients distinguished between awakening-first-then-powers and powers-first-then-awakening; one cannot say that once powers appear, one has awakened. For example, when Master Poshan of the Ming era cultivated at Tiantong, before he awakened he could already project his spirit to steal a villager's duck, playing at samādhi games. Later, when the matter came to light, Master Miyun Wu scolded him: “Your playful spiritual powers are not wanting, but you have not even dreamed of the Buddha-Dharma!” Poshan knelt and begged for instruction, and only after arduous further effort did he awaken. Coming down to modern times, the faculties of sentient beings are even poorer and their obstruction heavier; of those who would have powers first and awaken later, not one in ten thousand is to be found. Therefore we must, after awakening, practice relying on the awakening, gradually removing habits and gradually revealing powers. All the sages and patriarchs of old were without exception thus. Hence the two gates of sudden awakening and gradual practice are the norm for Buddhists, and followers of every school should practice and observe them!

Someone might say: Principle is precisely practice, and practice is precisely principle; principle and practice are not two. If principle is like sudden awakening, then practice should correspond accordingly; if in practical matters one still cannot pass through and there remain hindrances, how can it be said that one has awakened to the true principle!

Answer: Principle and practice are neither one nor different. Practice is accomplished through principle; principle is revealed through practice. Principle does not depart from practice, practice does not depart from principle; because of this non-separation, they are not different. But the true principle is formless, while its wondrous function follows conditions, responding to all things — falsely establishing empty forms that are not without shape; because of this presence and absence of form, they are not one. Now, when one has awakened, although one has clearly realized that one's own empty and still spiritual knowing is the true Buddha, yet because the habitual defilements of many lives are deep, they cannot be eradicated all at once; when meeting circumstances one still gives rise to thoughts, and before objects one can still hardly be without thought. But when thoughts arise, it is not as with the blind, who do not know that the dust-realms are originally empty, cling and grasp, wander and forget to return. Rather, when the previous thought stirs, the next thought is immediately aware and sweeps it empty. Only, compared with one who is wholly unmoved in mind, there remain traces of arising and ceasing, and the power is a little weaker. But if one can nurture and maintain it closely, constantly aware and observant, as days grow long and merit deepens, one will naturally merge it into one piece. The ox-herding practice of the patriarchs of old is precisely the model of effort after awakening.

The ancients said: Though sudden awakening makes one the equal of the Buddhas, yet the habitual tendencies of many lives are deep; the wind stops but the waves still surge, principle is revealed but thoughts still encroach. Therefore after awakening one must constantly watch. If false thoughts arise, do not follow them; reduce and reduce again until one reaches the unconditioned, and only then is it final. None of the good-knowledges under heaven who can manifest spiritual powers and transformations in their deeds have done so in a single day; they are gradually nurtured and revealed. Moreover, spiritual powers are matters of the very margin of sainthood, and in the eyes of the wise man they are not held in esteem; though they may arise, he does not wish to use them. If one has not reached the root — clear mind and seeing nature — but only seeks the branches — the manifestation of powers — not only can one not accomplish the Way, but one is bound for the demonic realm. This is something one must be careful about!

The Buddhists of today constantly measure others by spiritual powers, imagining that at the moment of awakening countless wondrous functions and spiritual powers forthwith appear, and that without such powers, though the eye of the Way be clear, one is still not awakened. Such people are indeed what one would call those who do not know root and branch, do not distinguish before and after — deluded and infatuated fools. They are themselves discouraged and do not believe in others; to cut off the Buddha-seed is nothing worse than this. How lamentable!

As for the second kind of chronic malady — holding that once one awakens all is done, with nothing to practice, nothing to attain, nothing to realize — compared with the former view that once one awakens powers appear, though it seems to have some awakening, yet because the view is not thorough, one has gone astray into a wrong path. The loss is the same as for those who have not awakened, and the harm may be even greater. For the former merely becomes self-discouraged, distrusting himself and others; but when the time and conditions arrive, he may still shatter his delusion and enter the proper track. The latter, however, believing himself to have awakened, has a deeply rooted wrong view, dispenses with later practice, and drifts on as before, sinking deeper into transmigration, with no power to extricate himself!

As said above, no-practice, no-attainment, no-realization belong to the side of principle, and are the final speech of those who have reached home; they are absolutely not reached at the moment of a single awakening. Especially for people of the present degenerate age, with poor faculties and heavy obstructions, one cannot, after awakening and without further cultivation, at once reach the state of effortless function. Those who say that there is no need to cultivate and that once one awakens all is over are either madmen or fools, and truly not to be believed.

For all sentient beings are originally endowed with the Tathagata's wisdom and virtue; only because of delusion and ignorance they do not know it, take the false as real, create karma and receive retribution, revolving through the six realms, reduced to sentient beings. Yet though in the state of a sentient being, their original nature is not lost; with a single awaking, they are no different from the Buddhas, not depending on contrived accomplishment — hence it is called no-practice. All forms are false and vain, originally empty and still, with not a single dharma — hence it is called no-attainment. At the ultimate ground even the Buddha is not established — hence it is called no-realization. But when the false habits have not yet been removed, and one clings and grasps, revolving in birth and death, one is not other than a sentient being. Therefore one must cultivate and nurture every thought, contemplate and illuminate every mind; after great awakening, with regard to evil, break evil and yet break without breaking (not clinging to marks); with regard to good, cultivate good and yet cultivate without cultivating — entering the hall and mounting the seat, returning home to sit at ease. This is what is meant by the “scholar of the unconditioned, the idle man,” and only then is it the time of no-practice, no-attainment, no-realization. If one has not reached this point and yet speaks loftily of no-practice, no-attainment, no-realization, is this not to deceive the worthy and cheat the sages, bringing grief upon oneself?
[The expression zi yi yi qi (
yi

) meaning self-invited sorrow, means bringing trouble upon oneself, inviting one's own grief. The first yi (zi yi, to leave or bequeath) means 'to bequeath or leave behind'; the second yi means 'this'; qi means 'sorrow, grief.'

Someone might say: Sudden awakening, sudden practice, sudden realization have existed since ancient times; does such a person not indeed awaken and be done? And does such a person also need gradual practice after awakening? If such persons have existed since ancient times, surely they are not lacking even now.

Answer: Those who awaken suddenly, practice suddenly and realize suddenly cannot enter unless they are persons of the highest faculties. To speak truthfully, the reason such persons' faculties are so high and deep is that in the past they practiced relying on awakening and accumulated through gradual nurturing; now, with their karmic conditions mature, they can awaken upon hearing and complete it all at once. On the surface it seems to be sudden awakening, sudden practice, sudden realization; in fact it is likewise the case of first awakening and then practice. The ancients said: Today's sudden is also yesterday's gradual. As for the present world, students' faculties are low and mean; unless they are great bodhisattvas returning, it is truly hard for them to suddenly awaken, suddenly practice, and suddenly realize. Even if there were one or two persons of great faculties who understand a thousand things upon one hearing and complete it all at once, they still cannot be without practice, without attainment, without realization. For the ignorance and habitual defilements cannot be finished in one lifetime; and how much more so, to speak of no-practice, no-attainment, no-realization — one has long since fallen into the midst of practice, attainment, and realization.

The Xiu Xin Jue says: “The common man, from beginningless kalpa, has revolved in the six realms, firmly grasping the self-mark, with false thoughts inverted, and the seeds and habits of ignorance, long established, have become nature. Though in this life he suddenly awakens to his own nature, originally empty and still, identical with the Buddha, yet these old habits are by no means easy to cut off. Hence when he meets favorable and adverse circumstances, with anger, joy, right and wrong blazing up and ceasing, the defilement of the guest-dust is no different from before. If he does not exert the power of prajñā to nurture and cultivate, how can he counter and purify it, and reach the ground of great rest and great cessation?”

Great Master Dahui Gao said: “Often those of sharp faculties, without expending much effort, settle the matter and then give rise to an attitude of ease, and do not cultivate further. As days and months grow long, they drift on as before, and inevitably fall into the cycle of transmigration. How can one, with a single period of awakening, dispense with later practice?”

Hence after awakening one must constantly observe and must not take it lightly. When a false thought suddenly arises, either a single alertness, or raising the Buddha-Recollection, until one reaches the unconditioned — only then is it final. Thus the meaning of sudden awakening and gradual practice is like the two wheels of a cart: lacking either one is insufficient.

Since sudden awakening and gradual practice are both the rule of cultivation and the bridge to the Way for Buddhists, how should one cultivate? And what difference is there from cultivation before awakening? Let me discuss this below.

(1) Cultivation after awakening cannot be spoken of uniformly; it must be determined by the depth of the student's false habits and the weight of his affliction. Those with shallow habits need no countermeasure; they merely go along with conditions, observing: when a thought arises, be aware of it; when aware, turn it to emptiness. Practicing thus from thought to thought, they naturally, little by little, attain the hundreds and thousands of samādhis. As the Xiu Xin Jue says: “Yet when one observes that delusion has no root, and thought by thought does not abide, the flowers of the three realms, like wind curling smoke, and the illusory six dusts, like soup melting ice, the defilement of the guest-dust naturally all turns into ambrosia.” If the student can thus practice from thought to thought, not forgetting to attend, holding concentration and wisdom equally, then love and hate will naturally grow faint, and wisdom will naturally grow and flourish. If the subtle continuous flow is eternally cut off, the great prajñā of perfect enlightenment will shine forth alone, and then one manifests the hundreds of thousands of billions of transformation-bodies, responding to conditions in the ten directions without hindrance.

The Xiu Xin Jue says: “Though one cultivates the ten thousand practices, yet one takes non-thought as the essential. All the good-knowledges under heaven, after awakening, practice the ox-herding; though there is later cultivation, yet they have already suddenly awakened — false thoughts are originally empty, the mind-nature is originally pure. Though they cut off evil habits, there is no evil habit to cut off; though they diligently cultivate merit and wisdom, there is no merit or wisdom to cultivate; cultivating without cultivating, cutting off without cutting off — this is true cultivation and true cutting off.”

It further says: “When seeing forms and hearing sounds, just be thus (that is, when seeing forms and hearing sounds, be like a bright mirror reflecting things, like the wind passing over trees, without giving rise to other thoughts); when dressing and eating, just be thus; when relieving oneself, just be thus; when meeting people and dealing with affairs, just be thus; and even in walking, standing, sitting and lying down, whether speaking or silent, whether joyful or angry, in every moment be thus in each of these. Like an empty boat riding the waves, rising and falling with the swell, yet thought after thought not abiding; like flowing water turning the mountain, meeting bends and meeting straights, yet with the mind utterly without knowing. Today buoyant and free, tomorrow free and buoyant; following all conditions, without obstruction, without hindrance; upright and without falsity, seeing and hearing as usual — then, not a single dust standing against you, what need of the work of driving and expelling? not a single thought giving rise to emotion, no need of the power of forgetting conditions.”

Such free-flowing still knowing, being originally the cultivation of the unconditioned, is in fact equal to no cultivation. It neither requires starting a new furnace to cling to Dharma and practice, nor reserving a still contemplation, taking stillness as practice — how completely at odds with cultivation before awakening, when one did not know the why and wherefore, firmly clung to the Dharma-marks, held fast to the rituals and rules, greedily sought merit and virtue, chased after tasks, and wore the shackles and chains of a prisoner!

(2) As for those with deep habitual defilements and great power of ignorance, who among good and evil, favorable and adverse states cannot help being swayed, whose minds are not serene — for these there is indeed the work of expelling false conditions and counteracting them. In the remedial methods, if agitation predominates, one should gather the scattered mind through the concentration-power appropriate to it; if drowsiness and dullness predominate, one should contemplate emptiness through the gate of wisdom (as to what type of practice is suitable, please see the next chapter, “The Ten Methods of Cultivation”). One must cause concentration and wisdom to be held equally, stillness and movement to annul each other, and enter the unconditioned; only then is it final. The Xiu Xin Jue says: “First, through the gate of concentration gather the agitation, causing the mind not to follow conditions, to accord with original stillness; next, through the gate of wisdom awaken the drowsiness, selecting the Dharma and contemplating emptiness, according with original knowing. Use concentration to govern chaotic thought; use wisdom to govern the indeterminate. When drowsiness and agitation mutually annul, and the remedial work is ended, then in the presence of objects, every thought returns to the essential; meeting conditions, every mind accords with the Way; practicing with free-flowing spontaneity in both, one is then without affairs.”
Someone might say: Such remedial cultivation is no different from the gradual practice of the inferior faculties before awakening — then what is the point of speaking of sudden awakening?

Answer: Because such persons have poor faculties and heavy habits, deep obstruction and thick defilement; though they too awaken to the self-nature's purity and emptiness, endowed with all virtues, the same as the Buddha, yet they are unable to face conditions without arousing feeling, and encountering conditions they become stoppered; being turned about by drowsiness and agitation, they are blinded to the still and constant knowing. Without relying on the remedial work to balance drowsiness and agitation, not only can they not enter the unconditioned, but they fall into delusion after awakening. One must be careful of this.
I will cite one or two kung-an cases of falling into delusion after awakening, to serve as a warning to those who, after awakening, still do not practice earnestly.

Elder Xian long studied under Xuedou, and after obtaining the Dharma, Xuedou intended to raise him to be abbot of Jine, but Xian would not comply. Later he went out to establish a monastery and lecture, and because the Elder Yuan of Deshan surpassed Xuedou in repute and fame, he changed to acknowledge Yuan as his teacher. Having the messenger carry letters to the various mountains, the old woman before the mountain gladly asked: “For whom does Elder Xian offer incense on his first ascent to the seat?” The envoy said: “For Elder Yuan of Deshan.” The old woman cursed him, saying: “Xuedou emptied his bowels and bladder to speak Zen to you, so that you have today's station — how can you be so ungrateful and unrighteous!”

Elder Jue of Kaisheng in Hezhou first studied under the Iron-Foot Fu of Changlu, and for a long time gained nothing. Later he went to the assembly of the Fifth Patriarch Yan of Dongshan and obtained the Dharma. Going out to reside at Kaisheng, he saw Changlu's assembly flourish greatly, and so changed to succeed Fu. Not acknowledging what he had received, when he offered incense he suddenly felt his chest pounded as if beaten, and an abscess grew into a fistulous opening at the painful spot. He plugged it with a cake of frankincense, and for a long time it did not heal — and at last he died!

Abbot Qing of Shu, well known in the monasteries, one day traveled together with Master Xiu into the capital to seek the Chan Master Fayun Yuantong. When they reached Fayun, Xiu was allowed to enter the hall and take lodging, but Abbot Qing was not granted permission. Qing was staying at Zhihai, and happened to fall ill. Xiu wished to ask after him, but the gate of the mountain gave no leave; so he secretly went to Zhihai to see Qing. Qing, in turn, wrote a letter to Yuantong, alleging that Xiu had gone in and out in violation of the rules. When Yuantong learned of it, at the night assembly he scolded: “Because of friendship and righteousness he risked expulsion to ask after your illness, and you in turn write a letter accusing him — is this what an upright man and true scholar would do?” When Qing heard this, he covered his breath. The whole monastery said that Qing died after a single scolding from Yuantong.

Attendant Ping of Dayang was a worthy disciple of the Chan Master Ming'an of the Caodong school. One day the Chan Master Yaoguangzhao came to visit, and Ming'an said to him: “He who will revitalize the Caodong lineage will be either Yuan or Jue.” Zhao said: “There is Attendant Ping.” An said: “Ping's old habits are deep.” And pointed at his chest, saying: “This place is not good either.” Then he pinched the fork of his thumb, showing it, and said: “In the future Ping will die right here.” When Ming'an passed away, Ping lived at Dayang and plotted to get the gold and silver that the commandant Li Hewen had given to his teacher, not hesitating to destroy the master's reliquary stupa. Though the elders of the mountain earnestly admonished him, he would not listen. When he opened the stupa, his teacher's face and countenance were as if alive; the wood was consumed and still he sat upright. All were astonished. Ping further struck open his teacher's skull, added more oil and wood, and in a moment it was reduced to ashes. The assembly reported this to the authorities, and Ping was convicted of plotting for the objects in the stupa, and for unfilial conduct was returned to lay life. Because of his bad character, all the quarters abandoned him. Ping drifted with nothing to rely on, and later was devoured by a great tiger at a three-forked crossing. And so he could not escape Ming'an's finger-fork prophecy. How sad!

Such kung-an cases are too many to enumerate in full; they are all cases where, after awakening, one did not rely on remedial practice and earnest cultivation, and with deep-rooted habits, blinded to one's conscience, was stirred to greed by profit and forgot kindness and righteousness — thus bringing it about.
