Of course, a man may give play to his wicked, fierce, crafty intelligence, but how can the Dharma-protectors be without mercy toward him? That he should come to no good end is only fitting!

One must know that though one borrows remedial work to temporarily adjust the habits, yet because one has first suddenly awakened to the mind-nature being originally pure and the afflictions being originally empty, one does not cling to the Dharma to cultivate, falling into the inferior view of practice, attainment, and realization. Hence one is able to return to the essential in every thought and accord with the Way in every mind, without losing the import of sudden awakening. Conversely, if one cultivates before awakening, because one has not seen the nature, though one nurtures and cultivates from thought to thought, yet in every step one gives rise to doubt; one cannot be free and unobstructed, and at the same time clings to Dharma-marks and grabs at merit and virtue, so that birth and death remain unended. Therefore, with the same remedial methods, for one who has awakened they are like a lodging borrowed overnight — a temporary expedient; he does not fall into attachment to the Dharma, and as days and months grow long, he naturally accords with the mystery of the Way and accomplishes supreme bodhi. This is no different from the prior sharp faculties with shallow habits, cultivating without cultivating, and not cultivating while cultivating — this too must be known.

Again, take the Pure Land followers who recite the Buddha's name. Before awakening, they do not know to return to the essential in every thought, but only seek outside, cultivating with attachment to form; some, worse, cling to the mark of merit, take quantity as superior, and rush through reciting sutras and mantras, till they actually bring on illness. After awakening, they know that mind is Buddha, Buddha is mind; to recite the Buddha is to recite the mind; to recite the mind is to recite Buddha. Reciting Buddha from thought to thought is awakening the original mind from thought to thought — what is called mind and Buddha meeting in the Way, fused into one piece. Hence the ancients said, only after seeing the nature can one lift the single phrase of the Buddha's name with its full force, because before awakening one neither knows where the recitation lands nor avoids giving rise to doubt at every step, and so does not obtain real benefit. After awakening, having recognized the root-origin of the mind, one may recite or not recite — there is no matter of reciting or not reciting; one neither clings to form to seek recitation nor avoids it and refuses to recite. All day long, naked and bare, free and at ease, following conditions without hindrance — only now can one truly be said to be successively continuing the pure thought, with not a single thought that is not a Buddha-thought.

Regarding the phrase “successive continuity of pure thought,” there is great learning in it. It is entirely the same as the preserving-and-nurturing effort after awakening in the Chan school, and it is the index of the recitation practitioner's course of cultivation. Not grudging the words, I will briefly discuss it below.

The two words “pure thought” are not, as the common run of people imagine, merely reciting the Buddha with a pure mind; rather, when the recitation is mature, the mind that recites and the Buddha that is recited fall away at once, subject and object both vanish, and emptiness and existence are both extinguished — this right thought alone is called pure thought.

As for “successive continuity,” it is further distinguished by the depth of the practice into continuity in stillness, continuity in movement, and the unity of stillness and movement. Let me analyze as follows.

1. Continuity in stillness. When a recitation practitioner recites to the point where subject and object both vanish and the nature manifests itself, this is the first manifestation of pure thought. Thereafter, because the marks and habits accumulated over the beginningless kalpas are deep, it cannot appear in every sitting, but must be separated by several weeks, months, or even a year before it appears again; this all depends on the practitioner's faculties and the density of his practice. At this point the practitioner must redouble his diligence, so that the interval gradually shortens — from a year to several months, then a month, then several days, and finally it appears in every sitting. This is continuity in stillness, corresponding to the first stage of the Chan school's “preserving (bao)” effort; it is principle-and-mind single-mindedness.

2. Continuity in movement. When one can be continuously within stillness, yet when encountering the turmoil of states and conditions it is again interrupted, it cannot be called true continuity. One must train in the midst of daily activity, until one is free and unobstructed in every direction, unconstrained by favorable and adverse, as if in stillness, still solitary and luminous, without a single slip — only then is it continuity in movement. But if one occasionally forgets, and on meeting a state one stirs, immediately one is aware and returns to emptiness. This corresponds to the second stage of the “preserving (bao)” effort; it is practice-and-mind single-mindedness.

3. Unity of stillness and movement. Whether in movement or in stillness, there is no slipping, and moreover no mind of keeping — purely letting nature take its course. This corresponds to the first stage of the Chan school's “letting go (ren)” effort; it is principle-and-practice single-mindedness.

4. Even continuity is unobtainable, and the mind of not-keeping is likewise gone; all the former mysteries and wonders are swept away at once, and all day long one is as if foolish and dull, tasteless; yet within the tastelessness there is an utmost flavor. This corresponds to the second stage of the “letting go (ren)” effort; it is the single-mindedness of relating to all things. This is true successive continuity of pure thought.

For the convenience of later students in choosing a method of practice, I will extract the ten methods of cultivation spoken of by the Elder Zhine of the Yuan era, and present them for everyone's reference.

Question: I do not understand, in the teaching lineage, what Dharma is used to govern the mind? Answer: Use the mind of no-mind to govern the false mind. Question: If a person has no mind, he is then the same as grass and trees. Please, for the saying “no-mind,” grant me an expedient explanation. Answer: What is now called “no-mind” is not that there is no mind-substance, which is then called no-mind; rather, when there is nothing in the mind, it is called no-mind. For example, an empty bottle: because there is nothing in the bottle, it is called an empty bottle — not that there is no bottle-substance, which is then called an empty bottle. Hence the patriarch said: You have only to be without affairs in the mind and without mind in affairs, then naturally empty and yet numinous, still and yet wondrous — this is the essential purport of this mind. According to this, then it is the removing of the false mind, not the absence of the true mind's wondrous function. From of old the various masters have spoken of the practice of no-mind, each in different ways; now I will gather the main points and briefly set out ten kinds.

1. Awareness (juecha). That is, when practicing, ordinarily be free of thoughts and guard against the arising of thoughts; when a single thought is just born, immediately break it with awareness — the previous thought being broken by awareness, the later thought does not arise. This awareness-wisdom also need not be used; false and awareness alike are forgotten — this is called no-mind. Hence the patriarch said: Do not fear the arising of thought; only fear that awareness be slow. And a verse says: Do not seek the truth; only cease your views. This is the practice of awareness that stills false thought.

2. Rest (xiuxi). That is, when practicing, think neither of good nor of evil; when the mind rises, let it rest; when one meets conditions, let it be still. Hence it is said: Go on like a single strip of white silk, go on cold and chilly, go on like the incense-burner in an old temple! Only when you have eliminated all fineness and separation, foolish and dull, do you have a little correspondence. This is the practice of resting the false mind.

3. Extinguishing the mind and preserving the state (minxin cunjing). That is, when practicing, when all false thoughts are stilled, do not heed the external states, but simply still your own mind. The false mind being stilled, what harm are the external states? This is the ancient's method of robbing the person but not the state. Pang the Layman said: Only be without mind toward the ten thousand things — what harm if the ten thousand things always surround you! This is the practice of extinguishing thought, stilling the false, and preserving the state.

4. Extinguishing the state and preserving the mind (minjing cunxin). That is, when practicing, observe all the internal and external states as empty and still, preserving only the single mind, solitary and upright, standing alone. Hence the ancients said: Do not be a companion to the ten thousand things, do not make a counterpart to the dusts; if the mind attaches to a state, then the mind itself is false — now since there is no state, what falsehood is there? This is the ancient's method of robbing the state but not the person. Hence it is said: The flowers of the upper garden have already fallen, while the chariots and horses still crowd and throng. This is the practice of extinguishing the state, preserving the mind, and stilling the false.

5. Extinguishing both mind and state (minxin minjing). That is, when practicing, first empty the external states, then extinguish the inner mind; since internal and external, mind and state, are both still, in the end whence does the false arise? Hence Guanxi said: The ten directions have no wall to lean on, and the four sides have no gate. This is the patriarch's method of robbing both the person and the state. Hence the saying: The clouds scatter, the waters flow away; the person is still, heaven and earth are empty! This is the practice of extinguishing mind and state and stilling the false.

6. Preserving both state and mind (cunjing cunxin). That is, when practicing, let the mind abide in its position and the state abide in its position. Sometimes when mind and state face each other, the mind does not run toward the state, the state does not approach the mind; each not reaching the other, naturally false thoughts do not arise, and one is without hindrance to the Way. Hence the sutra says: This Dharma abides in its Dharma-position; the marks of the world abide everlastingly. This is the patriarch's method of robbing neither the person nor the state. Hence the saying: A single moon rises over the sea, and several families go up the tower! This is the practice of preserving state and mind and extirpating the false.

7. The whole body within and without (neiwai quanti). That is, when practicing, mountains, rivers, the great earth, sun, moon and stars, the inner body and outer vessels, all the dharmas — are the same as the true-mind substance, serene and void and bright, without a hair's difference; the great chiliocosm of worlds of dust fused into one piece — where could one still obtain a false mind! Hence Master Zhao said: Heaven and earth share the same root with me; the ten thousand dharmas are of the same substance as I. This is the practice of the whole body within and without, extirpating the false.

8. The complete function within and without (neiwai quanyong). That is, when practicing, observe all the inner and outer body and mind, vessels and realms, all dharmas, and all functions and activities, as the wondrous function of the true mind; when all thoughts are just born, that is the wondrous function manifest. Since everything is wondrous function, where could the false mind take its seat? Hence Yongjia said: The real nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory empty body is the Dharma-body. This is the practice of the complete function within and without, stilling the false.

9. Substance is function, function is substance (jiti jiyong). That is, when practicing, though one is fused with the true substance, of one flavor of emptiness and stillness, yet within it there is hidden a numinous clarity — the substance is the function; within the numinous clarity there is hidden emptiness and stillness — the function is the substance. Hence Yongjia said: Alert and tranquil is right; alert and falsely attached is wrong. Tranquil and alert is right; tranquil and indeterminate is wrong. Since in the midst of tranquility the indeterminate is not allowed, and in alertness chaotic thought is not used, how can any false mind arise? This is the practice of substance-is-function, function-is-substance, extirpating the false.

10. Breaking through substance and function (touchu tiyong). That is, when practicing, do not distinguish within and without, and do not distinguish east, west, south, north; take all the four directions and eight quarters as a single great gate of liberation. Round and full, substance and function not divided, without a hair's leakage, the whole body fused into one piece. Where could the false arise? The ancients said: The whole body is without seam or gap, above and below forming a round — this is the practice of breaking through substance and function, extirpating the false.

Of the above ten kinds of practice, one need not do them all; if one achieves a single gate, the false will naturally be stilled and the true mind appear. According to the root conditions of one's past lives with which some dharma has affinity, practice it accordingly. This practice is the practice of no-work, not a work that is done with the mind's contrivance. Even if one practices them without having awakened the true mind, it is easy to see it at once. This method of stilling the false mind is most important for those who study the Way; hence, not disliking detail, I record it to show later students. Do not regard it as gilding the lily!

The above ten practices are all to be exerted in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; one must be in dressing and eating, in relieving oneself, in conversation and work, in every moment and every place, closely and subtly aware and observant, without the need for sitting meditation and investigating. If there are those whose habits and obstruction are deep and whose strength is insufficient, and who still need to sit in meditation, let them continue as they wish; but after rising from the seat, they should carry the meditative power onto the states and train it in movement, so that they may sooner fuse it into one piece, and reach the great work of no-work, perfecting the great Way of bodhi.

As for the esoteric school, after awakening one must still practice esoterically, in order to attain realization in this very body. The breadth of its methods and the numerousness of its expedients far surpass the exoteric school. But the esoteric Dharma values a master's transmission and abhiseka; it cannot be openly displayed, so I shall omit it.

blocks.text: 4. Realizing the Essence and Activating Its Function
(1) The States of Realizing the Essence

inline.s: As for the states of realizing the essence, the ancients for the most part did not speak fully. First, because this realization-state is beyond the reach of words and thought; as soon as it falls into verbal expression it is guilty of dwelling. Second, because one who truly realizes it returns to having nothing attained, and does not wish to show it off to others. Third, for fear that those who have not awakened might steal it for themselves and so delude others. Fourth, for fear that people might attach to the state and seek it, thereby obstructing the gate of awakening. Fifth, because the states passed through by each person are not entirely the same. For these various reasons, they only sketched it with words like “the clouds disperse, the long sky fully revealed,” “the clear sky without a single cloud for ten thousand li,” “the mind-moon solitary and round, its light containing all things,” “neither light nor dark, neither great nor small, neither blue nor yellow,” or even “round and round, bright and brilliant.” I now seem to be no exception; and moreover I have nothing realized, nothing attained, and am even less able to speak. I can only pick up a few ready-made kung-an sayings to offer the readers. As for the detailed circumstances, I leave them for the reader to strive, realize, and experience himself.

When we practice until subject and object are both forgotten, and mind and Dharma both extinguished — no matter what school we cultivate — then it is a sudden snap and a sudden burst, like an explosive suddenly detonating: within, body and mind; without, the world; and even space itself, all at once fall away and are shattered into nothing, even that “nothing” is nothing. This is what is called the great earth sinking flat (vanishing) and space being shattered. At that very time, though there is not a single thing possessed, yet it is void-bright, still and coagulated, with a single numinous awareness not extinguished, clearly knowing, not like wood or stone. And though it is clear, yet there is neither that which knows nor that which is known; because this clarity is entirely one single mass of void-bright numinous knowing, there can no longer be a knower and a known — for there to be further knowledge would be adding a head upon a head, and would no longer be this. After we realize this true state, turning back, we then recognize that this “numinous knowing” is nowhere else — all day long it shines from the gate of the six sense-roots, without the slightest separation or gap from us; all our speech, movement, and activity is nothing but its numinous, wondrous function. Formerly we went through a thousand hardships and a hundred kinds of seeking and searching; it was all along right before our eyes but unrecognized — and instead we defiled it, humiliated it, revolving in the six realms, suffering — is that not a wrong and a sorrow! The ancients said: “The phrase before the sound, the thousand sages do not transmit; the single thread before the eye, from ancient times without a seam.” And again: “Having worn out iron shoes in seeking it without finding, when found it costs not a single effort.” This is what they point to.

[The note “the phrase before the sound, the thousand sages do not transmit” — “the phrase before the sound” refers to the phrase before the sound is uttered, the phrase before father and mother gave birth to us; this is the Buddha and patriarchs' “treasury of the true Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa.” “The thousand sages” refers to the Buddhas and patriarchs who appeared in the past. It means that this “treasury of the true Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa” is neither a word nor a phrase, and could not be transmitted even by a thousand Buddhas and ten thousand patriarchs. It represents the great matter of the upward vehicle, which no one else can transmit, but which must be personally realized and attained through one's own realization. The Biyan Lu (Blue Cliff Record) says: “The phrase before the sound — the thousand sages do not transmit; never having personally seen it, it is as far as a great chiliocosm away.”

But this is only the plain Dharma-body; one must still diligently polish and grind, closely removing habits, before it can blaze forth in great light. When the practice is mature, even in deep sleep the crown of the head is bright with a full moon shining. When the light is pure and clear, the broad heavenly eye naturally opens, the ten directions world simultaneously illuminate, and I enter into all and all enter into me, like Indra's net, interpenetrating layer upon layer, with endless wondrous function.

Someone might say: Such states are realized by practitioners of the Chan or esoteric schools; followers of the Pure Land school who recite the Buddha's name should not be so, for they aim at rebirth in the Western Pure Land, and ought in concentration to see Amitābha Buddha and the Western sacred states, and should not be utterly without seeing. If one sees nothing at all, how can one be reborn in the Pure Land?

Answer: Have you not seen the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi of Master Yinguang recorded above? Master Yinguang is one who vigorously advocates relying on the Buddha's compassionate power to be received and led to rebirth in the West. Why then does he also say, in the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi, that no-seeing is true seeing, and that true seeing has nothing seen? Because the true Thusness Buddha-nature is without form or mark, unstained by a single dust, unsullied by a single thread; to say it is like any one thing is already not right. Hence the true Buddha truly has nothing to be said and no form to be seen. But this formless Buddha-nature is not blank nothingness; hence it can follow conditions to manifest marks and put forth function. But because the marks arise following conditions, they are only provisional names, not a real substance. Hence to see a Buddha with marks is not to see the true Buddha. The ancients said: The reward- and transformation-bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they the expounders of the Dharma. The Lotus Sutra calls them a phantom city, not the jewel-mansion. Those who wish a highest-grade, highest rebirth in the Western Pure Land must pass through the small resting-place of forms, and realize the true Buddha's markless wondrous body, before they can fulfill their wish. Conversely, clinging to a Buddha with form and a Pure Land with marks can only yield the lowest-grade rebirth; this is an immutable truth. Hence Master Yinguang, when speaking of the highest state of Buddha-recitation — the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi — could not but say that seeing-without-seeing is true seeing. For having realized such a profound and lofty state, mind and land are fused into one piece; mind is the land, the land is mind. To make the vow for rebirth in the West is just to be reborn in the Pure Land of one's own mind — to be reborn without a birth — and would one still fear not having the highest-grade rebirth?

After seeing the nature, if one stubbornly guards the state of emptiness, or indulges in dwelling in quietude, and does not know how to bring forth function amid circumstances, one is like a poor man who, having come into wealth, does not know how to use it and in the end remains as poor as before. Moreover, without being tempered amid things and circumstances, one cannot attain the great samādhi in which principle and phenomena are mutually fused, still less reach the realm of non-obstruction among all phenomena and accomplish the great merit of perfecting the Buddha Way. Therefore one must surely polish the principle one has awakened to amid things and circumstances, wearing away its sharp corners, before one can arrive at perfect wonder. Yet those who have just awakened often do not know the method of bringing forth function, and are still less clear about its process; some, because their strength is for the moment insufficient, waver when they meet with events, and then doubt that what they have awakened to is wrong, thereby shaking their very foundation. Bewildered and at a loss, they do not know what to do — how greatly to be regretted! Here I select the essential passages from The Process of Realizing the Essence and Activating Its Function, written by my late master Xianglu, and excerpt them below, to help readers, after awakening, bring forth the function of prajñā and accomplish the supreme merit of non-doing. How fortunate indeed!

The wondrous substance of true reality inherently possesses non-abiding wondrous function. The student must take the pure and free radiance he has realized and carry it into the midst of inverted human affairs, turning the existent back to emptiness, turning inversion into purity, turning affliction into freedom. Then he not only extinguishes his own suffering but can extinguish the suffering of others as well; this is what is called ferrying living beings across.

The deeper the practice, the more and the faster the habitual tendencies are stirred up. The student need not be afraid: these are seeds naturally turned up from the field of the eighth consciousness. Though they are stirred up quickly, they also pass away quickly; a stirring may be greater than usual, but each time one arises it becomes smaller, shorter, and fewer, and it never grows again.

The deeper the practice, the greater the courage. If one is suddenly startled, it is only a single start, and one is not startled again; moreover, the more the strength is used, the stronger it becomes.

The deeper the practice, the more one sometimes becomes very forgetful, and then again one’s memory becomes very strong, and one grows daily more agile. One’s power of perception also grows strong, and often one responds to things without deliberating — these are the forerunners of spiritual penetration.

Constantly observe this original nature and silently accord with it. The moment a habitual tendency arises, be aware of it; awareness turns it to emptiness. At the same time, use prajñā to sweep away this emptiness, and again use prajñā to sweep away that sweeping. When you have swept until there is nothing left to sweep, then you accord with the original nature, then you accord with the purport of prajñā’s great emptiness.

In practice one must be accurate, ruthless, reflective, patient, even, and steady. Accurate means seeing the direction clearly, without doubt or retreat. Ruthless means restraining oneself without the least leniency; not even the smallest fault of one’s own may be indulged. Reflective means constantly turning back and examining oneself. Patient means waiting for the time; without a considerable span of time, one’s strength cannot become sufficient. Even means contemplating all things as equal. For whatever obstruction there is arises from a mind that is not even, from discriminating gain and loss. Not knowing that dharmas are originally unborn, why worry about gain? Not knowing that dharmas are originally undying, why worry about loss? One who can be even is naturally unstartled, unafraid, and unawed, and passes beyond into the realm of freedom. People often have the mark of time, the mark of gain and loss, the mark of success and failure; when these various habitual tendencies come, they cannot break through them. This is insufficient samādhi and incomplete prajñā, that is to say, the power of prajñā is not strong. Hence one must be patient, and wait until the time comes; then the strength is naturally sufficient. It is like traveling a road: what matters is not to mistake the direction and to advance step by step, not to be fast or slow. Steady means being thus stable and never retreating.

The matter of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature is undertaken for the sake of birth and death throughout measureless kalpas — how momentous it is! One must never count mere intellectual understanding as sufficient. For what is gained by intellectual understanding, being wholly without samādhi-power, gives rise to mad wisdom and inversion, and in the end cannot be called illuminating the mind. Seven stages are distinguished here:

1. By exceedingly strong prajñā-power one sees the original nature, and from this attains a small measure of samādhi — as with those who enter through the Chan school. Or by strong samādhi-power one awakens prajñā and sees the original nature — as with those who enter through the practice of the mind-essence esoteric dharma.
2. Having seen it, one must deeply believe without doubt, and take up the burden as the first thing.

3. One sees that the nature pervades the dharma-realm, so that everything in the dharma-realm is nothing but the nature. Call it illusory, and all is illusory; call it real, and all is real. Ultimately, the real and the illusory alike are only provisional names, without substantial reality; when the mind can be unfettered by them, this is called non-abiding.
4. Abiding in nothing at all, one is empty yet does not fall into annihilation, for wondrous function is plainly present. The illusory mind is not nonexistent — this is called non-arising.

5. Though it is called non-abiding, one is not without clear knowledge and discrimination of good and evil; one merely discriminates without abiding, and so enters the realm of equality and non-duality.
6. When the mind is equal, there is naturally no obstruction and no fear, and one is free wherever one goes.

7. One’s strength repeatedly advances and retreats, now samādhi, now prajñā; later, samādhi and prajñā are no longer divided, and one only advances and never retreats. This is truly to have illuminated the mind and fused principle and phenomena.

After illuminating the mind, the “view of self” is not immediately removed, nor are habitual tendencies immediately purified. That the view of self and habitual tendencies come again and again, and that again and again one can turn and transform them — this is what it is to be one who has truly illuminated the mind. If the power of transformation is slight, that is another question. The only fear is not knowing how to turn and not knowing how to transform; then one cannot turn or transform at all. Hence in learning the Buddha Way, the first thing is to open one’s awareness, as if gaining wealth; the second is to make good use of that awareness, as if spending wealth; the third is to empty even the awareness; the fourth is to have no notion of empty or not empty, for it is originally thus. It is like a man of true wealth and nobility, who of himself forgets his many possessions.
Once illumination and awareness arise, habitual tendencies dissolve; but here the speed differs from person to person. There are ten stages in this:
1. Circumstances come and one is unaware.
2. Circumstances come and only afterward is one aware, and the arising of awareness is exceedingly laborious.
3. When circumstances come, the arising of awareness is not difficult.
4. Circumstances come and awareness arises at once, with only a slight before and after.
5. Circumstance and awareness arise together, yet sometimes awareness is lost.
6. They arise together, and one need not lose it.
7. Awareness precedes the circumstance, though sometimes it comes after, or now and then one actually slips back to forgetting.
8. Awareness is constant and unmoving.
9. The awareness is not yet pure.
10. Ever still and ever illumining, even the awareness no longer abides — this is when one’s strength is truly sufficient.

From of old, gross habitual tendencies are easy to shed while subtle ones are hard to remove; this too is inequality. Hence there still remain the fruits of startle, terror, and fear. In between, one may suddenly rise and suddenly fall, but this must not be called retrogression.

In ordinary times, constantly use the method of turning the light back to examine your own habits. Whether good or bad, virtuous or evil, whatever is not easily transformed and removed belongs to the root of birth and death; never stubbornly hold to it as good and keep it. The harder it is to transform, the more you must transform it. To constantly go against yourself — that is the advance of practice.

Removing habitual tendencies is like a battle between humans and gods; only after a hundred battles can one win, for it is by no means the work of a single morning or evening. Only after illuminating the mind does one have the qualification to give battle; this is the activating of function — from small battles to great battles, from small victories to great victories, until the enemy is routed at the root and there is never any trouble again.

In practice, one absolutely must not suppress and must not evade. The roots of greed and anger must be pulled out and dissolved. If one only knows to guard precepts, samādhi, and prajñā and to use them as antidotes to greed, anger, and delusion, then the two views of good and evil leave their shadows in the mind. It is like defending a city when the enemy comes: though for a time the enemy cannot enter, he has not gone away, and seizing his chance he can still enter the city — this is not ultimate. Therefore do not suppress and do not evade; better to break through, so that neither leaves a shadow. When the mind is stained by nothing, enemy and self dissolve into one, and one enters the great samādhi.

When circumstances come, one pays them no heed and does not give rise to thoughts, yet does not fall into annihilation — this is samādhi in stillness. Facing circumstances without confusion, one still responds, moving yet unmoving — this is samādhi in movement. When movement and stillness are one and the same, and there is nothing that must be and nothing that must not be, then it is the great samādhi.

In training the mind one must train the mechanism, and this lies in thoroughly understanding the principle of cause and effect. Constantly bring forth contemplation; when the practice is mature, the great mechanism and the great function arise. All affliction comes from affection and views. Affection is self-love, view is self-clinging; when affection and views are solid, they become a covering obstruction, and the mechanism that observes causes and penetrates effects is no longer efficacious. This is why the working of the mechanism does not arise.

One who attains the penetration of others’ minds relies precisely on the swift, lively mechanism that observes causes and penetrates effects; hence principle and phenomena are perfectly interfused, and without deliberation everything is seen distinctly. It all lies in the twin endowment of samādhi and prajñā and in the maturing of practice. This itself is spiritual penetration — there is no sort of marvel to be sought elsewhere.

If one is willing to do the tasks one disdains, willing to say the words one dislikes saying, and willing to receive the people one is unwilling to meet, then one is not far from the light of equal wisdom.
To see the faults of others not only makes it hard to enter non-duality; it also obstructs one’s own holy path and gives rise to arrogance — what those who cultivate the Way most abhor!

When practice becomes intense and urgent, there must be a period in which one is unversed in the ways of the world and human feeling; hence it is said to be “as if one had lost father and mother.” For when the urgency reaches its height, one is bound to fail in etiquette and deportment. People often do not forgive this, calling it arrogance and self-importance, or suspecting one of madness. This is a stage everyone must pass through, and it is hard to argue about.
When in practice one is now diligent and now indolent, seeming to advance and seeming to retreat, do not doubt or resent it; this is the time of advancing, and you must not be impatient and dejected.
To delight in quiet and loathe commotion is inequality, and is utterly impermissible; know that quiet and commotion are discriminations of your own mind and have nothing to do with circumstances.

For one who cultivates the Way to praise himself and disparage others, to belittle others and magnify himself, is the most shameful and laughable of things; beware lest those of understanding mock you!
Make vows not rashly, for to make a vow is easy while to fulfill it is hard. The vow should be great and firm; into one’s own mind not the slightest trace of affection or view may be mixed.
Of the eight winds in which one remains unmoved, four winds are easy to guard
(decline, defamation, ridicule, suffering)
, while four winds are hard to fend off
(gain, honor, praise, joy)

, for the adverse are easy to know, whereas the favorable often catch one in their snare without one’s knowing it. Hence in matters that go as one wishes, one must be all the more on guard, lest they sweep one into their toils.

[The eight winds] gain, decline, defamation, honor, praise, ridicule, suffering, joy. Gain is what makes one elated; decline is what makes one dejected. Defamation is being slandered behind one’s back; honor is being praised behind one’s back. Praise is being extolled to one’s face; ridicule is being mocked to one’s face. Suffering is the various pains of body and mind; joy is the various pleasures of body and mind. Because these eight dharmas are always loved and hated by worldly people, and can moreover stir the human heart, they are likened to “the eight winds.”

In this there is nothing extraordinary — only the removal of habitual tendencies. Do not take it as saintliness! What are called the mysterious and the supernaturally transformative are also loose and ordinary; it is only because one has seen little that one marvels much, takes it for mystery, forgets the original nature, and enters the demonic path — is that not a pity!
In practice, never measure your strengths and weaknesses against others; rather, silently observe and examine yourself.

The method of practice is a temporary expedient; never cling to the method. To crave the Dharma is the same as to crave fame and profit — the same birth and death. To become a Buddha means to accomplish the emptiness of nature that is the Buddha’s. When the mind clings to anything, it at once loses the original nature and departs from the Buddha’s realm; hence one should be vigilant and aware at all times.

The removal of habitual tendencies also depends on causes and conditions, and so differs in speed. After illuminating the mind, preserve and nurture it closely (by “preserving and nurturing” is meant: never press the mind down into inactivity; simply be able to transform without abiding). After a considerable period, there is the wonder of habitual tendencies suddenly dissolving away.

The countless miseries of living beings come from one word alone: turmoil. Turmoil arises from inferential cognition. One who has seen the nature is perfectly clear in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: when no thought moves, the mind’s confrontation with objects is direct perception; and when thought moves and discriminates, it moves yet does not move, so that even the inferential is also direct perception. To be constantly able to be thus is called becoming one piece.

The measure of one’s power of skillful means turns with the measure of one’s prajñā-power, and the measure of prajñā-power depends on whether contemplation is perfect or not. Perfect, and it is unobstructed; unobstructed, and it is perfect. What is called unobstructed means that the mind is without hindrance; hindrance means using the mind to hinder the mind. When the mind is bright and perfect and undeluded, it is unobstructed; this is called the unimpeded wisdom, and it is set forth in the Great Compassion Heart Dharani. A dharani is the mind’s place of utmost emptiness and utmost subtlety.

The method of training the mind lies simply in bearing patiently what hinders. Take all one’s habits: they have no fixed definition, and nothing is really impermissible. The trouble is that one has formed the habit and thinks it must be so, and so cannot bear to go against oneself — this is how the hindrance is set up. If one can bear it, then there is no hindrance, for originally there is none. Take matters of “face,” for instance: they are illusory and unreal; at most one loses an illusory face! Just see whether it really hinders or not. It is merely a moment’s discomfort, and when one has overcome it after all, the unimpeded prajñā-power one gains — could it be bought for ten thousand pieces of gold! Hence learning the Buddha Way is the work of a great man: able to bear, able to let go, neither drifting with the world nor quarreling with it — what is called “harmonious yet distinct,” whereby one transcends and enters sagehood.

The scenes that appear in dreams can serve to test the depth of one’s practice. Whenever practice reaches a close and dense intensity, the mind responds in dreams. To have mastery within a dream is proof that one will not fall into the three evil paths. For falling into the three evil paths must have as its cause the mind losing its mastery: having only the power of following and no power of mastery, one follows karma up and down and enters without being aware. Moreover, if one has a single measure of strength in a dream, one must have ten measures when awake. Mind and body are half separated in dream and wholly separated at death; death and dream are not greatly different.

Because all wondrous function is not apart from worldly awareness, after illuminating the mind and seeing the nature one must be attentive everywhere to human feeling and worldly affairs, practicing until one is thoroughly versed in them, and using them to remove habitual tendencies on both sides. Only when one is familiar with the principle of cause and effect can one gain the initiative of the mechanism and bring forth the great working of the mechanism.
The Mahavairocana Sutra

Abiding Mind Chapter Commentary, says: “When a bodhisattva first awakens to the Way, he immediately attains in this life the samādhi that removes the covering obstructions; he dwells together with Buddhas and bodhisattvas, develops the five spiritual penetrations, gains the dharani of understanding the languages of all living beings, can know the mental actions of all living beings, and performs the Buddha’s work to ferry them across far and wide,” and so on. To awaken to the Way is to see the nature and become a Buddha; to remove the covering obstructions is to remove habitual tendencies. When habitual tendencies are pure, at that time the five spiritual penetrations open forth — they cannot be sought in advance. After gaining the penetrations, one uses the penetration of others’ minds as skillful means to liberate living beings. This is the process of realizing the essence and activating its function; those who do not enter by this path are outsiders.

After awakening to the Way, though the five spiritual penetrations may not all open forth at once, one is no longer an ordinary person; for having realized the root, all the removal of covering obstructions and the opening of the penetrations develop simultaneously — only the power is still slight.

“Awakened, one is still the same as before awakening” — unless one arrives at plainness, the furnace fire cannot turn pure blue. This is what is meant by “great wisdom appears foolish”: all day long as if dazed and simple, one becomes one piece.

What has been recorded above is truly a ford and bridge for bringing forth the wondrous function of prajñā after illuminating the mind and seeing the nature. If students can indeed enter with faith and without doubt, then after realizing the essence, keeping themselves stirred and alert at every moment, tempering themselves amid human feeling and worldly affairs, deeply comprehending the mental actions of living beings, and becoming familiar with the principle of cause and effect, they will remove the covering obstructions, open the five spiritual penetrations, and bring forth the great working of the great mechanism.

[Covering obstructions] means the five coverings. [The five coverings] are five kinds of affliction. “Covering” is another name for affliction, because affliction can cover over people’s mind-nature and prevent good dharmas from arising. The five coverings are: desire, hatred, torpor and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt about the Dharma. [Restlessness and remorse]: restlessness (the mind wavering, not still) and remorse. Both of these mental states keep the mind from peace and bring affliction. [Doubt about the Dharma]: doubting that the Dharma one has received is the true and correct path, and therefore not revering, believing, accepting, and practicing it. [The five spiritual penetrations] are also called the five penetrations, or the five supernormal transformations, namely: the penetration of the heavenly eye, the penetration of the heavenly ear, the penetration of others’ minds, the penetration of past lives, and the penetration of the power to appear at will. The penetration of the heavenly eye means having cultivated an eye-faculty equal to that of the gods of the form realm; one who has it can see regardless of distance or nearness, inside or outside, day or night. The penetration of the heavenly ear means having cultivated an ear-faculty equal to that of the gods of the form realm; one who has it can hear every sound. The penetration of others’ minds is the spiritual penetration that enables one to know all the thoughts of others; one who has it need not fear being plotted against in secret. The penetration of past lives is the ability to know one’s own past births and deaths within the six realms and to know the past births and deaths of the living beings of the six realms within the six realms; one who has it can recall all the affairs of past lives as clearly as if pointing at the palm of his hand. The penetration of the power to appear at will is also called the penetration of spiritual realms, or the penetration of the spiritual feet; one who has it can have everything as he wishes — drilling into the sky, entering the earth, moving mountains, overturning seas, scattering beans to become soldiers, calling the wind, summoning the rain, mounting the clouds, riding the mist — none of it is any problem.

blocks.text: 5. The Question of the Final Destination

inline.s: A visitor asked where one who has illuminated the mind and seen the nature goes after entering parinirvāṇa; another asked about the Sixth Patriarch’s words at his entry into quiescence, “I myself know where I am going,” noting that he did not say clearly where — was it that he knew and did not speak, or that he did not know where and so did not speak?

Where one is reborn at the end of life is indeed a crucial question for a cultivator. If one does not get it clear, it will greatly hinder the progress of practice and will also bring detours in the fruits of realization to come.

Generally speaking, the myriad living beings bob up and down in the six realms, revolving without cease, dying and being born, without knowing why. Now that one has awakened, recognized one’s own mind, and seen one’s own nature, one ought to know where birth comes from and where death returns to. If one is likewise muddled and ignorant, is that not a reckless self-conceit that takes the unawakened for the awakened?

But what is called birth and death, coming and going, is spoken with regard to deluded people who cling to marks. As for one who is awakened, having opened the true eye and thoroughly seen the true mind, the three realms and the six realms are all unreal, and the Pure Lands of the ten directions are like the moon in water. Since it is originally unborn, how can there be extinction? Since it is originally undying, how can there be birth? Birth and death being absent, how can there be coming and going? And how can there be any place at all?

After awakening to the Way, the Sixth Patriarch said: “How unexpected that the self-nature is originally pure! How unexpected that the self-nature is originally unborn and undying! How unexpected that the self-nature is originally complete in itself! How unexpected that the self-nature is originally unmoving! How unexpected that the self-nature can produce all dharmas!” What is called illuminating the mind and seeing the nature is precisely seeing this true nature of true emptiness and wondrous existence, which is unmoving, neither coming nor going, unborn and undying, and yet can manifest marks according to conditions and bring forth all kinds of wondrous function. Since one has clearly seen that the self-nature is unborn and undying and neither coming nor going, why should one then take from it the marks of coming and going, birth and death, and have somewhere to go? Therefore, to speak of a life ending and a rebirth taking place is in fact not yet to have awakened and seen the nature.

The Sixth Patriarch’s saying, “I myself know where I am going,” was like picking up a yellow leaf to stop a child’s crying. His not saying clearly where he was going was because in truth there is nowhere to go. For this nature is like space — what place of return does space have? If one sees a place to go, one falls into the concrete and clings to marks. Falling into the concrete and clinging to marks, birth and death are not ended. With nowhere to go, one can go anywhere; one can go anywhere and yet has never gone. What is called returning is no returning, and no returning is returning; everywhere is a return, and wherever one arrives is the return.

Again: wondrous existence is true emptiness — because it is wondrous existence; otherwise it would be blank emptiness. True emptiness is wondrous existence — because it is true emptiness; otherwise it would be delusive existence. Therefore one who thoroughly awakens to the mind-nature fuses form and emptiness and secretly unites essence and function; neither leaning toward emptiness nor clinging to existence, in the place of no birth and death one may freely manifest birth and death: though born, yet unborn; unborn, yet not without birth. Hence in the heavens above and on the earth below, among the four kinds of birth and the six realms, and even in the Pure Lands of the ten directions, there is nowhere one cannot be born. In the place of neither coming nor going, one may freely bob up and down; though manifesting a body everywhere, in truth there is no coming or going — no coming or going, yet constantly coming and going. It is not to be a dead, unmoving thing sitting behind the black mountain and claiming to have no birth, death, coming, or going.
Layman Pang’s Verses on the Unborn say: “A son who takes no bride, / a daughter who takes no groom; / the whole family gathered inside, / all speaking of the unborn.”
The Chan master replied in harmony: “No son who needs a bride, / no daughter who needs a groom; / the great assembly gathered inside — / what talk of the unborn!”
I ventured to reply in harmony: “A son may take a bride, / a daughter may take a groom; / sons’ sons and grandsons beside — / this is to speak of the unborn.”
The three verses together precisely reveal this nature of true emptiness and wondrous existence: no birth and no non-birth, nowhere present and nowhere absent.

One who has truly seen the nature is free according to conditions, clinging to no mark whatsoever, making no distinction between pure and defiled, ordinary and sage, no difference among the four kinds of birth and the six realms. What are called birth and death, coming and going, are all a samādhi of play, not established as real existence. If it is so, what need is there to point to a definite place to go?

For instance, a monk asked Changsha, “Where did Nanquan go when he passed away?” Changsha said, “In the east house he becomes a donkey; in the west house he becomes a horse!” Another monk asked, “Where did Nanquan go when he passed away?” Changsha said, “If you want to ride, ride; if you want to dismount, dismount.” Still another monk asked, “Where did Nanquan go when he passed away?” Changsha said, “When Shitou was a novice, he went to pay his respects to the Sixth Patriarch.” The monk asked again, and he said, “Tell him to go and ponder it.” When he asked three more times afterward, Changsha was silent three times. What praise this gives to the wondrous nature of true suchness — so elusively appearing and vanishing, inconceivable, impossible to lay hold of anywhere! When Sansheng (a Dharma heir of Chan master Linji) heard this, he said, “This reply of Changsha may be called unprecedented and unrepeatable, rarely heard in ancient or modern times!” From this one can see that the numinous knowing wondrous nature is omnipresent. We need only put everything down, without the slightest abiding, and not seek a place of presence; then everywhere is presence, and wherever we dwell we are constantly at ease.

But one who has clearly awakened to the self-nature, if old habits are deep and thick and in daily activity he cannot be unconstrained by favorable and adverse conditions or unstained by sound and form, then segmentary birth and death is not yet ended, and he cannot yet be as carefree and free as described above; he must still go back and forth between the human and heavenly realms seven times, or three times, before attaining freedom. On this point Chan master Guifeng, according to the depth of practice, distinguished three kinds of freedom, urging students to strive diligently. First, if deluded thoughts arise, one does not follow any of them; at the approach of death, karma naturally cannot bind one, and though there is an intermediate state, one goes where one wishes, entrusting oneself at will to the heavens or the human world. This is the freedom of receiving birth. Second, if thoughts of love and hate have been dissolved, one is no longer subject to a segmentary body, and can of oneself change the short into the long and the coarse into the fine. This is the freedom of transformation. Third, if the subtle outflows are all stilled and extinguished, and only the great perfect-enlightenment wisdom remains luminous and alone, then one manifests a thousand hundred billion transformation bodies according to circumstances to ferry across living beings who have the connection — this is called a Buddha. This is ultimate freedom.

Fellow practitioners, after clearly awakening to the original nature we should guard and sustain it strictly, strive to advance, and with unremitting diligence exhaust the present karmic outflowing consciousness, so as to reach ultimate freedom and attain the supreme fruit. We must never be satisfied with a little and, halting our progress, drift downward. Should our strength fall short of our intention and the conditions not come together, we should still strive to attain the freedom of transformation. If even this cannot be done, then there is nothing for it but to vow to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, or the Inner Court of Tusita, or other Buddha-lands and Pure Lands, in the hope of being freed from the two kinds of birth and death and realizing the true and eternal. Since the Ming dynasty, many Chan masters, such as Lianchi and Chewu, have made the vow for rebirth in the Western Pure Land after their awakening — perhaps it was precisely because they could not attain the freedom of transformation that they were compelled to vow rebirth in the Pure Land.

Those who practice the mind-essence esoteric dharma, if they fear they cannot accomplish it perfectly in this life, recite, in addition to their practice, the root mantra of Maitreya Bodhisattva forty-nine times each day, thus laying the foundation for future rebirth in Tusita and ensuring advance without retreat — their diligence of mind is bitter indeed.

Of course, the ordinary being of great aspiration, for the sake of ferrying living beings across, fears not birth and death and looks upon falling into the three evil paths as falling into the four sage realms, with no sign of reluctance. Such a one is truly a great man whose noble resolve soars to the clouds, revered by gods and humans alike and protected with approval by Buddhas and bodhisattvas; he is not included in the above case.

Above I have rambled on about the meaning of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature and the means of realizing it, introduced the skillful means of true cultivation after awakening, and further recounted the process of realizing the essence and activating its function, quoting in passing from the writings of several ancient and recent great masters. It would seem that the Dharma-gate of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature, of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation, of accomplishing it all in one lifetime, has been described exhaustively, leaving nothing out. Yet to speak thoroughly and truthfully, all of this is idle talk that dulls living beings, not worth mentioning, a superfluous effort. For all living beings are originally Buddhas; there is no need to cultivate, no need to realize. They are originally possessed of boundless wondrous function and unimpeded spiritual penetration; if they simply let things run their course, dressing and eating, responding to conditions and meeting things, neither grasping nor rejecting, neither attaching nor seeking, then they are the Thus-Come Buddha just as they are.

Patriarch Linji said: That which before your eyes is vividly present, without a single form or segment, solitary and bright (that is, before the eyes there is a formless, markless brightness, clear yet empty, vividly uninterrupted and absolutely without a counterpart) — this is the living Buddha, the living patriarch. He also said: Your single thought of pure mind-light is the Dharmakaya Buddha; your single thought of non-discriminating mind-light is the Sambhogakaya Buddha; your single thought of non-differentiating mind-light is the Nirmanakaya Buddha. He also said: This mountain monk’s insight is no different from Śākyamuni’s; in daily life there are so many uses — what is lacking? The numinous light of the six realms (that is, the functioning of the six sense-roots) has never paused for an instant — if this is not Buddha, what is?

If we can, amid all affairs and conditions, be without turning toward or away, without grasping or rejecting, responding with ease and mastery, free in both letting go and taking hold, then laughter and anger, jest and scolding are all wondrous spiritual function, and walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are all the ocean-seal radiating light. For what is called numinous is that whatever one does is the functioning of the true mind’s numinous light: all scenes and marks are manifested by it, and all achievements are accomplished by none other than it. What is called penetrating is to be without obstruction, without blockage or stoppage — that is, amid things and circumstances to be without hate or love, without joy or sorrow. If it is so, then body and mind are light and quick, transcending the dust of defilement, neither mind nor Buddha; when hungry, eat; when tired, sleep — what is there left to cultivate?

Yet alas, living beings do not cast a glance at the ground beneath their feet: either they chase scenes and pursue objects, clinging to marks and running in search, or else they are heavy with deluded thoughts and deep in affection and views. Thus they have put the Buddhas to trouble, so that they appear in the world, chattering and prattling, talking of long and short, mixing mud with water and stooping into the weeds, until one would like to have them struck dead with Yunmen’s staff and fed to the dogs, and so bring peace to the world. But the Buddhas’ compassion is urgent: unafraid of being blamed, undaunted by being struck dead, they still come in vast procession, giving away head, eyes, and marrow for living beings. Where there was no opening for speech, they provisionally spoke the twelve divisions of the teaching; where there was no place to lay hold, they established eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates — all simply in the wish that we might awaken from the dream of delusion, go home along the road, and recover our original face. Their care and pains were bitter indeed!

If, after this detailed and lucid account, we still cannot bite it firmly and dare not affirm that “one’s own mind is Buddha,” or even fail to understand that dressing and eating are themselves wondrous spiritual function and instead fix upon something strange and mysterious, then we must not only recite the Buddha’s name and practice Chan with diligence and hardship, but must all the more devoutly cultivate the esoteric methods, so as from samādhi to open prajñā and awaken to the original nature; only then can we go on to preserve and nurture it, remove habitual tendencies, sit securely at home, and be freed from birth and death. We must never blindly prate of no cultivation, no attainment, and no realization, thereby ruining this whole life and bringing misfortune upon future lives! Still less should we shrink back before difficulty and let the good opportunity slip away.

What are called spiritual penetrations and transformations are in fact quite ordinary, for they are the wondrous function inherent in the nature, not something coming from outside. Only because in ordinary times they are obscured by deluded thoughts do they not appear; now, once delusion is exhausted and they shine forth, because one has seen little one marvels much and thinks them mysterious and unfathomable. In truth everyone possesses them and everyone can do them, just as everyone can dress and eat — what is so extraordinary? The ancients said that falling into the three evil paths is the same as falling into the four sage realms; the ten dharma-realms are all alike in spiritual penetration and transformation — what is there to prize, what is there to wonder at? Moreover, as soon as one fixates on the strange and bizarre, one enters the demonic path — this too one must be careful about.

As for practicing no-thought, one must by no means press thoughts down so that they do not arise; rather, when thoughts arise, do not follow them and do not climb after conditions, and do not abide in the marks of objects. People are not wood or stone — how can they be without thought! To become a Buddha is to be an awakened one of great mechanism and great function, lively and exquisite — how much less can such a one be without arising thoughts! Hence the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment teaches us: “At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts, yet do not extinguish the deluded mind either.” The Diamond Sutra says: “One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere.” And the Sixth Patriarch’s verse to save Wolun from extinguishing the mind says: “Huineng has no contrivance at all, / he cuts off not a hundred thoughts; / facing objects the mind rises many times — / how then does bodhi grow!” Therefore we need only keep the mind empty at all times, neither grasping nor rejecting anything, not stirring emotional thoughts; we may go on responding to conditions and meeting things, yet we do not perceive a mind arising to respond, and after the matter is done there is not even a trace of mental effort. Thus all day long one moves and yet has never moved; all day long one gives rise to thoughts and yet not a single thought has arisen. Chan master Lanrong’s Song of No-Mind says: “Just when the mind is used, / just then no mind is used; / with no mind, just so it is used — / in constant use, just so, no mind.” Truly this is the finest portrait of no-mind.

Again, practicing no-thought does not mean taking as progress the gradual lengthening of the time of true emptiness and no-thought between the cutting off of the preceding thought and the non-arising of the following thought — as if today no-thought lasted only a minute, and one slowly extends it to five minutes, ten minutes, and even an hour or twenty-four hours, and that is success. Know that no-thought is vividly alive, not rigid like a block of wood or stone. A monk asked Zhaozhou, “What is no-thought?” Zhaozhou said, “Hitting a ball on rushing water!” Later someone offered the words: “Thought after thought without lingering!” What is called no-thought is not that not a single thought arises; rather, thoughts arise and cease as they arise, without the slightest trace of abiding marks. Hence, as said above, just when a thought arises in response to conditions, one does not perceive the thought arising; and since there is no arising, how can there be ceasing? Without birth and death, it is called no-thought. When one is not responding to conditions and meeting things, though not a single thought arises, it is only like treading on a tiger’s tail or walking on spring ice: it stirs the moment conditions meet it, and is not like wood or stone, dead, still, and without knowing.

Someone may ask: Today’s exposition is very detailed, and I deeply believe that the void-still numinous knowing when not a single thought arises is our true nature. But why is it that I still cannot see through every one of the Chan gongan?

Answer: The Chan gongan are nothing very extraordinary either; they simply test whether a student can avoid being taken in and robbed by circumstances, whether he can avoid establishing views and being deceived by phrases, and whether he can avoid falling into annihilation and remain ample and at ease in the working of the mechanism. The student need only, after recognizing the root, preserve and nurture it closely, and prajñā will naturally open day by day, the light of wisdom will naturally grow rounder and fuller day by day, and he need not worry that he will not understand these sayings. As it is said: “Gain the root, and the branches need not worry you; fear only that you do not become a Buddha — do not fear that a Buddha cannot understand your words!” The words and phrases of the Chan school do not deliberately set up oddities or play with the mysterious and empty; they are used to test whether a student’s mechanism is sharp or dull and to observe the strength of his daily realization and of his care for the original nature. Hence we need only practice deeply in ordinary times, so that the mind is like great space, and not be taken in by its mechanism and circumstances; then, with the mind empty and abiding nowhere at all times and in all places, our response to the mechanism will naturally be swift. Any phrase or gongan, the moment it meets the eye, is known for what it is. For example, when Chan master Weishan Lingyou addressed the assembly: “A hundred years from now, this old monk will be born as a water buffalo in a donor’s house at the foot of the mountain, and on its right flank will be written, ‘A certain monk of Weishan.’ Call me a monk of Weishan, and it is a water buffalo; call me a water buffalo, and it is a monk of Weishan. What will you call me?” This is using the two names, water buffalo and monk of Weishan, to swap your eyes around, to see whether you are taken in or not. If your mind is not empty and pure and you do your business on names and marks, you will certainly be deceived by his “buffalo” and “monk,” and once you establish views on names and marks, you have been taken in by his mechanism and circumstances! Therefore you must use the method of shedding, and come out with words that leave aside “buffalo” and “monk,” and only then is there a road out. For what is called monk and what is called buffalo are both merely temporary false marks and false names; speaking from the true nature, where is there buffalo or monk? Hence, fixing your eye on the true, with not a single thing established, you break out through the encircling siege. At that time no one in Weishan’s assembly could answer, but afterward an old worthy answered very well. He said, “The master has no other name!” Though he did not speak of a name, he did not depart from names; having said that originally there is no name, he yet allowed that any name may be given at will; neither attaching to monk and buffalo nor departing from monk and buffalo, he both pierced through names and marks and revealed true suchness, and yet true suchness is not apart from these names and marks to be something else. Truly a doubly-pivoted wondrous saying! But now we too need not let the ancients monopolize the beauty; let us offer another phrase in repayment to the ancients. Since the wondrous function of the nature is boundless, one may turn it sideways or stand it upright and depict it at will, and need not be confined to one pattern. The above answer speaks from the essence; we may now change and speak from the function: “An idle name has always filled the five lakes!” Do you worthy ones understand? And tell me — is this the same as the former saying, or different?

Again, when the Chan master Gaofeng asked his students, 'Why does a great cultivator of the mind not observe the vinaya?' it too was to test whether the student was bound by names and forms. And in the same way one need only answer him with the method of shedding: 'Because he does not know good from bad!' For the Buddha-nature is pure and undefiled, hung upon not a single thread, free of good and evil. What is there of precepts or no-precepts, of wisdom or no-wisdom?! To speak of precepts, of concentration, of wisdom is to gouge a sore in sound flesh, bringing only pain and toil!

Moreover, even if one's speech is smooth and one's replies are subtle and wondrous, one must still be carefully examined before one knows whether it is true awakening. For some Chan practitioners, having read a few gongan from books or caught some ready turns of phrase from other people's lips, steal them as their own and play them upon their tongues; when by chance they hit upon a phrase that matches the expected answer, they take themselves to have awakened. That is a great, great mistake!

Thus when the Chan master Xuefeng Yicun ascended the hall and addressed the assembly, saying, 'As to this matter, it is like an ancient mirror: when a barbarian comes, a barbarian appears; when a Han comes, a Han appears,' Xuansha stepped forth and asked, 'And what if all at once the mirror itself should come?' The master said, 'Barbarian and Han both vanish!' Xuansha said, 'The abbot's heels do not touch the ground!' In this way he would not approve of Xuefeng. Recently a Chan student said, 'Why not answer him, "Break the mirror and come to see!"?' The words are indeed very fine. But one must examine whether he truly has insight. So I pressed him further, asking, 'Once the mirror is broken, how do you come to see?' Whereupon he was struck dumb and could offer no answer. Such fit phrases, as one can see, do not flow forth from one's own breast but are picked up by hearsay from outside. This is what the master Guizong called toad Chan, which can hop only a single hop. The ancients said, 'A single fit phrase becomes the stake that ties the donkey for ten thousand ages!' How can one not tremble at this!

Again, the master Miyun Wu of Tiantong Temple, at the winter solstice, bid his attendant take a padded robe to an elder dwelling in a grass hut to ward off the cold. The elder said to the attendant, 'This old monk has the robe born with his own mother; I have no need of a winter garment.' The attendant returned and reported this to Miyun Wu. Wu said, 'This monk appears to have some awakening, but I fear it is not yet real; search further beneath his words.' He therefore told the attendant to go again and ask, 'Before your mother bore you, what garment did you wear?' The elder could make no reply. Wu told him to investigate this phrase. Three years later the monk passed away, still without an answer. At his cremation there were countless relics, and the whole assembly gasped in amazement. Wu said, 'Ten measures of relics are not worth a single turning phrase. Try to answer in his stead.' The assembly was all silent. This gongan shows that a phrase which merely resembles the truth is not true awakening, and that relics after cremation are not realization of the Way. One must truly know one's own mind and see one's own nature, and then one is like a gourd pressed beneath the water, which spins the moment it is touched, perfectly fused without obstruction, lively and free. Now, to repay my readers and settle this gongan, and not shrinking from exposing my own weakness in broad daylight, I will answer in their place: when asked 'what garment did you wear before your mother bore you?' one need only reply, 'The tender peach and plum have just withered, and chrysanthemum and plum blossom are fresh anew!' And this spares him too the stir of Miyun's probing.

We must not force ourselves into the role of clever interpreter and, having gotten a smattering of half-understanding on the path of reasoning, take complacent delight in it and suppose we have awakened to the Way. One must practice earnestly in the hidden and secure place. Even if we cannot for a while fathom these gongan, it is of no great consequence; so long as we have genuinely recognized the original mind and guard it strictly, so that thought after thought is not different and mindfulness upon mindfulness is without lapse, diligently removing false habits and remaking ourselves, then within three or five years we are sure to bring about 'the skin falls off entirely, and only the one reality is revealed!' These old monks' tongues need not be feared to fail in piercing in seven places and penetrating in eight: however you take them up, whatever way you turn them, all become wondrous truths. For these sayings, and all supernormal powers and wondrous functions, are nothing but idle furniture within his own self-nature mind; what is there strange about them, what is there to esteem and rely upon! Moreover, the one who truly arrives home finds nothing to gain in returning. It is called no Buddha and no living being, no realization and no attainment! If there is the least trace of mystery, a touch of the marvelous, one is already settled upon a realm; far from being able to become a Buddha, one is rather on the way to being seized by a demon! It is a pity that some well-known people of today are likewise settled upon supernormal powers and functions, their minds not yet tranquil and pure. When they comment on the ancients and the moderns, either they say a man's supernormal powers were great, or they say he had no ability, without pointing out the very place where they clung and attached, so that later students might know the goal to pursue and be spurred onward. This shows exactly that they still have something they hold dear and fall into a rut; how can one speak of this without being stirred to a thousand feelings!

Now, for the convenience of later students in distinguishing the true mind from the false mind, so that they may know to press forward with vigor and not wrongly enter a devious path, I herewith transcribe below the section on distinguishing the true and false from the Straight Talk on the True Mind composed by the Chan master Zhina.

It is asked: When the true mind and the false mind confront an object, how does one distinguish them? It is answered: The false mind, confronting an object, has knowing and yet knows; with regard to agreeable and disagreeable objects it gives rise to greed and anger, and with regard to neutral objects it gives rise to delusion. Since upon an object it gives rise to the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion, that shows it clearly to be the false mind. As for the true mind, it knows without knowing. Because its serene mind is an even, complete illumination, it differs from grass and trees; because it does not give rise to aversion or attachment, it differs from the false mind. That is, facing an object with emptiness and clarity, neither hating nor loving, knowing without knowing, this is the true mind. Therefore the Zhaolun says: Now the sage's mind is subtle and without form, so that it cannot be called existent; yet the more it is used the more it is present, so that it cannot be called non-existent. Being not existent, therefore it knows without knowing; being not non-existent, therefore it knows without knowing. Hence knowledge without knowing is itself knowing, and there is no way to speak of it as different from the sage's mind.

Again, the false mind, when there is something, is attached to something; when there is nothing, is attached to nothing. It constantly dwells on one of the two extremes and does not know the middle way. Yongjia says: Abandoning the false mind and seeking the true principle, the very mind of abandoning and seeking becomes a cunning falsity; students who do not understand apply themselves to practice and truly come to recognize a thief as their own son. As for the true mind, it dwells in existence and non-existence yet does not fall into either, always abiding in the middle way. Hence the patriarchs said: Do not chase after the conditions of existence, do not dwell in the patience of emptiness; in one even and serene mind, it is all absorbed and exhausts itself. The Zhaolun says: Therefore the sage dwells in existence yet is not existent; dwells in non-existence yet is not non-existent. Though he does not grasp at existence and non-existence, he does not abandon them either. And so he blends his light with the dust, turns amid the five destinies, goes in stillness, comes in calm, tranquil and without effort, and yet does nothing left undone.

Again, the true mind is the ordinary mind, and the false mind is the un-ordinary mind. It is asked: What is called the ordinary mind? It is answered: Every person possesses a point of numinous clarity, limpid as empty space, pervading everywhere. Toward worldly affairs it is provisionally named reason-nature; toward false consciousness it is provisionally named the true mind. Without the slightest discrimination, encountering matters it is never dull; without a single thought of grasping or rejecting, touching objects it is everywhere complete. It does not chase after the shifting of the myriad realms; even if it flow along with them and gain the wonder, it does not depart from the limpidity of its own place; seek it and you come to know you do not see it. This is the true mind. It is asked: What is called the un-ordinary mind? It is answered: Among objects there are the ordinary and the sage, the defiled and the pure, the severed and the eternal, the arising and the ceasing, the moving and the still, the going and the coming, the good and the ugly, the beautiful and the vile, and so on down to the thousand differences and the myriad distinctions; all are called un-ordinary objects. The mind that follows these un-ordinary objects and arises and ceases, set against the aforementioned ordinary true mind, is called the un-ordinary false mind. It is asked: Does the true mind, being ordinary, never arise? It is answered: The true mind is sometimes put to use, but it does not arise in pursuit of objects; it is only a wondrous functioning in play, never obscuring cause and effect! Let students take these words to heart three times over!

Finally, let me still offer students one loyal word of advice. After we have recognized the true mind and realized the original nature, we must still practice all good deeds: first, to temper our own habitual tendencies and so increase the light of wisdom; second, to accumulate merit and fortune and so make provisions for becoming a Buddha. For although the essential nature of our suchness is pure, the habitual contamination of the beginningless long kalpas is not yet removed; and without the perfuming of various expedient means, the afflictions can never become pure. And this defilement of afflictions pervades everywhere, so one must cultivate every kind of good conduct as its antidote. Moreover, the Buddha is the Honored of the Two Endowments, fully rounded in both wisdom and merit; only then can one become a Buddha. If one has wisdom alone and no merit, one is merely an arhat and cannot become a Buddha. Therefore one must widely practice all the good and accumulate merit and fortune. Never take pride in one's heavenly innocence and fail to cultivate the many good conducts, thereby falling into sloth and mistakenly sinking into the evil realms, so as to commit a grave error!

But when cultivating the good, one must accord with the mind of no-mind and not grasp at the reward of merit. If one grasps at the reward of merit, one falls among the rewards of humans and devas, is hard put to realize suchness, and does not escape birth-and-death. If one accords with the mind of no-mind, then it is an expedient means to Buddhahood. Not only does one transcend birth-and-death, one further comes into the possession of vast merit and fortune. The Diamond Sutra says: 'The bodhisattva who gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and fortune is immeasurable and unthinkable!' This is a saying for which a thousand pieces of gold cannot be exchanged.

At the last, in play I have matched a ci lyric, to the tune 'Treading on the Grass,' with the verses of Qin Guan and Tao Zhu on 'The Post Station at Chenzhou,' to bring this essay to a close. In olden days Chenzhou was desolate and thinly peopled, a place of banishment and exile. Because of the disputes over reform, Shaoyou was banished to dwell there, and his spirit was darkened with grief; hence the mood of his verse is steeped in sadness and bitterness, in longing for the past and remembrance of old friends. As for Tao Zhu's verse, since Chenzhou has now been built into a thriving and flourishing place, with industry advanced and the surroundings beautiful, he opens a broad and generous heart, and returns the verse with a contrary meaning, so its mood is bold, bright, spirited, and rich in color. Both verses appeared in the press and were for a time much admired. Now, gathering the import of the two, I match them with one more, to show that the Buddha Dharma is not apart from worldly dharma, and that worldly dharma is precisely the Buddha Dharma. It may serve to help you gentlemen temper yourselves amid the circumstances of the world, remove the hindrances of habit, perfectly realize bodhi, and shine brilliantly in the midst of worldly affairs. Wherever I fall short, I ask my readers to correct me generously.
Mist veils the towers, / green floods the ferry crossing; / the Peach Blossom Spring lies not apart from the ordinary place!
The realm has no good or ill, yet the mind draws its line; / let it unfold of itself, and raise no scaffold of views!
The bridge leaps a long rainbow, / the fish brings its woven letter; / the scenery is of itself a measureless store!
Riding conditions, free and open, at ease in sink or float, / glad to become the spring mud that guards every blooming flower.

Having written to this point, I could not help bursting into a great laugh! Suddenly I heard someone say, 'What are you laughing at? Do you not fear that once you open your mouth you can never close it again?' Glaring sternly, I shouted back, 'Who has seen me open my mouth!' And so it is:
I have told all the feeling of cloud, hill, and tide,
lips unstirred, no thought that strays aside;
The jade hare quickens, and the clam holds the moon,
the clay ox sinks to the sea, and the wooden dragon croons its tune!
